#9751. Building a Kubernetes Operator for Workload Identity Federation Across AWS and GCP

My name is Shankar, working as a Devops Engineer in Santa Clara, CA. Developed https://Myceliam.dev.

My name is Shankar, working as a Devops Engineer in Santa Clara, CA. Developed https://Myceliam.dev.

My name is Shankar, working as a Devops Engineer in Santa Clara, CA. Developed https://Myceliam.dev.

Most clusters I've worked on have at least one pod with an AWS access key or a GCP service-account JSON key sitting in a Kubernetes Secret. Someone minted it, someone copied it in, and nobody is sure when it last rotated.

Clouds providers have had a better answer for years. AWS has AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity and GCP has Workload Identity Federation. The workload presents a JWT from an issuer the cloud trusts and gets back credentials that expire in minutes. The catch is the setup.

For one pod in namespace payments that needs S3 in one AWS account and GCS in one GCP project, you need:

Now multiply that by namespaces, clusters and accounts. I tried Terraform first. It's a poor fit here because the inputs (ServiceAccounts) are created by app teams at deploy time, not by the platform pipeline. And the drift I care about, like someone editing a trust policy in the console, happens outside any pipeline. The cluster already knows which workloads exist, so I made the cluster reconcile everything else.

Myceliam is a Kubernetes operator that makes the federated path the easy one.

Kubernetes trusts its own ServiceAccount tokens. IDPs (Identiy providers) Keycloak, Auth0, and SPIRE each issue JWTs they're willing to vouch for. Public clouds like AWS and GCP will happily accept a federated token — from an identity provider they've already been told to trust. Each of those three systems already knows how to trust something. None of them know about each other by default.

Myceliam is named after mycelium, the hidden underground fungal network that connects separate organisms and lets them trade nutrients. In the same way, Myceliam is a Kubernetes operator that weaves identity threads between clusters, identity providers and clouds. It watches namespace and ServiceAccount events and creates the matching resources in IdPs and cloud IAM on demand, so workloads can exchange short-lived credentials to access cloud resources.

The core idea is a fixed mapping from Kubernetes constructs to identity-provider and cloud constructs. Everything is derived from names, so the operator never needs a database:

No per-namespace container; one shared Resource Server per cloud, --

IAM OIDC provider per account, keyed by issuer URL

WLI provider -- in a shared pool

ClientIDList entry + one tagged trust-policy statement per role

workloadIdentityUser binding on each target SA

Myceliam operator supports SPIFFE, Keycloak and Auth0 for IdPs, AWS and GCP for cloud providers.

The user-facing interface is deliberately small: labels on a ServiceAccount, plus a namespaced CRD per cloud that lists which roles or service accounts the namespace may federate into.

A label alone is not enough. A single AutoidpAllowlist object (myceliam-system/default) lists the namespaces the operator may provision. If it doesn't exist, every namespace is allowed, so a first install works with zero config. Once it exists, only listed namespaces get new provisioning, and removing a namespace from it never blocks cleanup of what's already there. Who can write that one object, controlled with ordinary RBAC, is the real security boundary. Without it, anyone who can create a ServiceAccount could trigger provisioning in an external IdP and cloud account.

Trust, not authorization. The operator registers issuers and writes trust statements. It never attaches a permissions policy or grants an IAM role. If a role or GCP service account listed in a profile doesn't exist yet, the operator creates it with no permissions, as long as MYCELIAM_AUTO_CREATE_PRINCIPAL is true (the default). Auto-creation exists because AWS won't create a role with an empty trust policy, so pre-provisioning meant hand-writing exactly the statement the operator writes anyway. Teams that want to own role creation can set the flag to false, and a missing principal then fails that ServiceAccount's reconcile with a terminal error instead. GCP's default compute service accounts can't be created this way, so those must already exist. Either way, the operator's own credentials need permission to create roles and service accounts. Keeping the operator out of "what can this identity do" limits its blast radius to "who can assume what".

No per-SA role selection inside a profile. Every ServiceAccount that references a profile gets the same targets. If you need finer access, you split the profile. That keeps the CRD trivial to read in a code review.

An issuer in the middle, not just the cluster's own. Every Kubernetes cluster already runs an OIDC issuer for its ServiceAccount tokens, and you can register it directly with AWS and GCP. That works, but the cluster signs every namespace's tokens with one key set, and every cluster's issuer has to be registered in every target cloud account, which grows into a mesh. Putting a Keycloak realm per namespace, an Auth0 tenant or a SPIRE trust domain in between gives per-namespace signing keys (with Keycloak) and turns the mesh into hub and spoke: the clouds trust a handful of issuers instead of every cluster.

From there, the operator takes over — and keeps taking over, on a timer, not just once:

That reconcile loop is the part that matters most. The CRDs aren't a setup script you run once — they're the desired state, continuously enforced. Someone rotates a client secret by hand in the Keycloak console, or edits a trust policy directly in the AWS console? The next reconcile (default: every 300 seconds) puts it back. There's no drift to notice three weeks later during an audit.

The detail worth sitting with: Myceliam is only in steps one and two. It never proxies, mints, or even sees the workload's actual cloud credentials — once the trust is registered, the workload talks to the identity provider and to AWS directly, and asks for its own short-lived token at request time. The operator's job stops at making sure that handshake can happen.

The operator needs admin access to Keycloak or Auth0 and credentials in every cloud account. It would be ironic to solve that with a static key, but there's a real chicken-and-egg problem.

The operator is written in Go on controller-runtime, with one reconciler each for ServiceAccounts, Namespaces, the two AccessProfile CRDs, credential Secrets and the allowlist. Four pieces of plumbing ended up mattering more than I expected.

1. Retryable vs. terminal errors. Every call to Keycloak, Auth0, IAM or GCP can fail in one of two ways. A missing config or a malformed label is permanent: retrying won't fix it. A 503 or "client not created yet" is temporary. I defined two error types, operr.Permanent and operr.Temporary (which carries its own retry delay), and translate them into a ctrl.Result in one place:

2. Finalizers. Without a finalizer, a deleted ServiceAccount is gone before you can clean up its Keycloak client and trust statements. ServiceAccounts, Namespaces and both AccessProfile CRDs get myceliam.io/finalizer, and cleanup runs before it's removed.

3. Knowing what changed. If someone removes the aws-access-profile label, the operator has to remove that SA's trust statements. But a reconcile only sees the current object, not the previous one. So after each successful reconcile, the operator stores the last-applied state in an annotation. It's scoped to the four fields that matter, so unrelated label changes don't churn it:

4. Periodic resync. Drift on the IdP or cloud side produces no Kubernetes event. Every successful reconcile requeues itself after MYCELIAM_RECONCILE_INTERVAL_SECONDS (default 300), so a trust policy edited in the console or a secret rotated by hand in Keycloak gets put back within five minutes.

Keycloak and Auth0 model the world very differently, so I pushed the differences behind one interface. This is trimmed from the real one:

tenantID is a neutral stand-in for "whatever this IdP isolates a namespace with". The odd return value on EnsureAccessScope exists because of an AWS behavior covered below.

Each namespace gets a realm, and each ServiceAccount gets a client whose client_id is forced to the SA name. Keycloak always sets azp to the client_id, so every token's azp claim reliably names the ServiceAccount. I didn't need a custom mapper for that, and it turned out to be the most useful property in the whole system.

Cloud audiences come from client scopes. The operator creates one scope per (cloud, SA), named -, with an audience mapper, and attaches it as an optional scope. The name doesn't need the namespace in it, because a realm already is one namespace.

A token carries the AWS audience only when the workload explicitly asks for it, and the example app fetches one token per cloud:

Auth0 has one tenant per deployment, assigns its own opaque client_id, and Resource Servers (APIs) aren't something you want one of per ServiceAccount. So the Auth0 provider uses one shared Resource Server per (cloud, cluster, namespace), and the per-SA Client Grants are what actually scope access.

That leaves a problem: nothing in an Auth0 token says which ServiceAccount it belongs to. The fix is a tenant-wide Action on the credentials-exchange trigger that copies values the operator stores in each Application's metadata into the token:

The operator manages the Action like any other resource. It creates it if missing, compares the deployed code to the embedded script on every reconcile, and re-deploys if they differ. The aws.amazon.com/tags block looks odd here, and the AWS section explains it.

For client-type: signedjwt, the workload authenticates with private_key_jwt (RFC 7523) instead of a shared secret. If a kubernetes.io/tls secret already exists (for example from cert-manager), the operator reads tls.crt. Otherwise it generates an RSA keypair and a self-signed cert. Either way it pushes the public key to the IdP, and an edited tls.crt is re-uploaded on the next reconcile.

Two details cost me time. First, Keycloak takes a JWKS, but Auth0's credentials endpoint takes a raw PEM and assigns its own kid (an RFC 7638 thumbprint). The interface therefore returns actualKid, and callers persist that rather than the value they computed. Second, I write client_id and kid to a separate -metadata secret so the TLS secret stays a pure kubernetes.io/tls secret that cert-manager is happy to own.

Registering the IdP is a get-or-create on the IAM OIDC provider, followed by adding whichever ClientIDList entries are missing. The interesting part is the role trust policy.

A role may already trust ec2.amazonaws.com, or another namespace's workload. The operator must touch only its own statement. I model just enough of the policy document to find statements by Sid, and I derive the Sid deterministically, because IAM only allows alphanumerics there and namespaces and SPIFFE IDs are full of hyphens and slashes:

upsertStatement replaces the matching Sid in place, or appends it, and returns false if nothing changed, so no write happens.

Bug I shipped: that "nothing changed" check used reflect.DeepEqual against the decoded existing policy. A JSON array decoded into any comes back as []any, but I was building conditions as []string. They never compared equal, so every reconcile rewrote every trust policy. The fix was to build the statement with []any throughout. It's an easy bug to miss because everything still works. It just isn't idempotent.

This one cost the most debugging time. When a token carries an azp claim, AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity checks the OIDC provider's ClientIDList against azp, not aud. Inside the trust policy, the :aud condition key also resolves to azp's value. I confirmed live that this happens even when aud is a single string. Get it wrong and you get a bare InvalidIdentityToken or AccessDenied with no hint, even when the signature, issuer and thumbprint are all correct.

Keycloak and Auth0 client-credentials tokens always carry azp. SPIRE JWT-SVIDs never do. So the operator writes an OR-match on :aud that accepts either shape. For Auth0 and SPIFFE it also adds a separate identity condition, because the namespace-shared audience doesn't prove which ServiceAccount is calling:

With no azp, AWS falls back to aud and refuses a token with more than one audience (Token audience contains more than one audience while authorized party is not present). GCP would accept one combined token, but AWS won't. A SPIFFE workload that needs both clouds therefore fetches two single-audience JWT-SVIDs. A Keycloak token could safely carry both audiences, because azp is always there, but all three example apps fetch one token per cloud so they work the same way.

A condition on :myceliam_service_account never matched, even though the claim was in the JWT with exactly the right value. :sub and :aud conditions on the same token worked. My best explanation is that AWS only exposes claims listed in the provider's discovery document (claims_supported), and a claim injected at runtime never appears there.

The workaround is AWS session tags. The Action writes the same values into the reserved https://aws.amazon.com/tags claim. The trust policy then matches aws:RequestTag/myceliam_service_account and grants sts:TagSession alongside sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity. I verified it in both directions: a matching value succeeds, a mismatched one fails, and a Deny keyed on the tag really blocks calls. Two traps here:

Auth0's iss is https://{domain}/ with a trailing slash. The IAM OIDC provider URL must match exactly, and AWS doesn't normalize it.

My first version gave each Keycloak ServiceAccount its own AWS audience (aws--), a namespace-wide one for GCP, and a third convention for Auth0. Three schemes for one concept were hard to reason about and harder to explain. Audiences are now always --: shared by every SA in the namespace, and never shared across clouds or clusters, because both are part of the string. That only works because the audience is no longer what proves identity. On AWS, the per-SA check is azp folded into :aud for Keycloak, the session-tag condition for Auth0, and sub for SPIFFE. On GCP it's google.subject plus the per-principal binding.

Every SA adds a statement to each role it targets. A popular role eventually hits the trust-policy size quota (LimitExceeded: Cannot exceed quota for ACLSizePerRole). The operator doesn't prune stale statements yet. That's next on my list.

I call the IAM REST API directly rather than using the Go SDK, mainly to avoid Application Default Credentials. The operator already has its own short-lived GCP token and just uses it as a bearer token.

Each GCP project gets one shared Workload Identity Pool, and each namespace gets one provider per identity source inside it. Provider IDs must be 4–32 lowercase characters, and the cluster ID is part of the name, so truncation needs care:

If SPIRE already issues identities, there's no IdP object to create. The operator only registers the SPIRE issuer with AWS and GCP and uses sub, the full SPIFFE ID such as spiffe://example.org/ns/payments/sa/checkout, as the identity claim. It's the simplest path in the codebase and the best illustration of the operator's actual job: it doesn't issue identity, it makes existing identity legible to the clouds.

The operator is out of the picture once trust exists. It never proxies, mints or sees cloud credentials. The workload gets a token from its IdP and exchanges it directly. On AWS, no ambient credentials are needed for the STS call:

On GCP it's two hops: an RFC 8693 token exchange at sts.googleapis.com, then generateAccessToken to impersonate the target service account:

The repo has two small example apps, one OIDC and one SPIFFE, that do exactly this and list real S3 and GCS buckets. I used them as my end-to-end smoke test after every change.

This is early-stage software. Known gaps: no automatic pruning of stale trust-policy statements, no expiry-based rotation for operator-generated signed-JWT keypairs (rotation happens only when tls.crt changes), single-instance operation only, and SPIRE must already be installed. Cloud providers are still parallel packages rather than an interface like the IdP side. Tightening that is the prerequisite for adding Azure and OCI.

My name is Shankar, working as a Devops Engineer in Santa Clara, CA. Developed https://Myceliam.dev.

A few months ago, we added private data to the Open ASR Leaderboard: 11 splits from Appen and DataOceanAI covering scripted and conversational speech from five accents (blog). The community response was great, with many highlighting the importance of held-out sets for trustworthy evaluations. Since then, we added one more private split for Indian-accented English with Voice Arena (blog).

We’re excited to announce a new collaboration with Liva AI to add even more private data with two new accents: Egyptian 🇪🇬 and Nigerian 🇳🇬.

This is part of our continued effort to improve representation in ASR evals (more accents and more languages) and to improve trust (new private data to minimize benchmaxxing, and new data providers). We’re excited to see the community continuing to push ASR performance for the world 🤗

With these new accents, we can now present a richer breakdown of accents, based on Kachru’s Three Circles (kudos to Hume AI for this idea in their leaderboard). The Open ASR Leaderboard will now report:

As more accents join, we’ll split the Outer and Expanding Circles.

Liva AI collects multimodal interaction data through consumer products used by real people. Because Liva owns both the collection environment and distribution, it can design products around specific model gaps across domains, industries, languages, modalities, and interaction types. This gives it access to natural, high-context behavior that emerges through real product use, rather than artificially elicited or task-based interactions.

#9749. Mise à jour SteamVR : la qualité d'image progresse — et la biologie structurale en VR devient enfin crédible

Valve a publié une mise à jour bêta de SteamVR qui améliore la qualité d'image diffusée vers tous les casques autonomes compatibles Steam Link. Concrètement, Steam Link — l'application de streaming dédiée de SteamVR — permet de jouer à sa bibliothèque Steam sur un Meta Quest, un HTC Vive Focus ou un casque PICO grand public via le Wi-Fi. Cette bêta pousse la netteté et la stabilité de l'image streamée sur l'ensemble de ces appareils.

Je me souviens d'une soirée d'hiver, l'année dernière, dans mon petit appartement mal chauffé. Je venais de passer trois heures sur un rendu de site de liaison, à zoomer et dézoomer sur un écran 27 pouces, la nuque en compote. J'avais téléchargé Steam Link par curiosité, appairé mon Quest, et lancé un viewer moléculaire quelconque. L'image était… floue. Les hélices tremblaient. J'ai tout débranché, un peu déçu. Ce soir-là, j'ai compris que la VR scientifique n'était pas qu'une question de logiciel : c'était aussi une question de pipeline d'affichage.

Cette mise à jour bêta de SteamVR change discrètement cette équation. Et pour ceux d'entre nous qui passent leurs journées à manipuler des structures protéiques, ça mérite qu'on s'y arrête.

Pendant des décennies, la biologie structurale s'est pratiquée sur écran plat. Un fichier PDB, un rendu Mol*, une souris, un clavier. C'est puissant, c'est reproductible, et c'est indispensable. Mais un écran plat impose une distance : la molécule reste un objet regardé, jamais un espace habité.

La réalité virtuelle change la question. Dans un casque, on ne regarde pas une protéine : on se tient dedans. Les boucles de la chaîne principale passent au-dessus de votre tête. Une poche de liaison devient un volume où l'on peut physiquement entrer. Deux résidus éloignés dans un rendu 2D deviennent deux objets à portée de main.

Encore faut-il que l'image suive. Une structure moléculaire est un objet dense : hélices, feuillets, chaînes latérales, volumes de densité électronique. Une image floue, un streaming qui saccade, et l'avantage spatial s'effondre. C'est précisément là que cette bêta SteamVR compte : elle lève un obstacle technique qui freinait l'usage sérieux de la VR pour la visualisation scientifique.

NexoPeek est un laboratoire moléculaire VR conçu pour Meta Quest. Il s'organise autour de deux usages complémentaires.

D'un côté, 12 visites guidées narrées, réparties en 6 piliers : biotechnologie de base, fondements du vivant, voies et interactions, médicaments en action, technologies génétiques, biotech verte. On entre dans l'hémoglobine pour regarder l'oxygène se fixer. On suit la dégradation du glucose dans la glycolyse. On voit l'aspirine bloquer les enzymes COX. On observe CRISPR-Cas9 éditer l'ADN.

De l'autre, un lecteur PDB professionnel. Une barre de recherche intelligente résout un nom de gène à travers RCSB PDB, UniProtKB, AlphaFold DB, SWISS-MODEL et PDBe, puis charge la structure à l'échelle humaine. Les presets Mol* d'un seul geste font défiler les représentations : cartoon, boules et bâtonnets, spacefill CPK, surface moléculaire, carte de facteur B, trace en tube. Les fichiers locaux (.pdb, .cif, .mol2) se chargent avec cartes de champ électrostatique et volumes de densité électronique.

Sur le banc d'analyse, les mains nues (ou les manettes) saisissent, mettent à l'échelle et font tourner la molécule. La prédiction de poches par IA met en évidence un site druggable lumineux — via l'IA cloud PrankWeb / P2Rank ou un moteur hors ligne. Foldseek superpose un homologue. L'inspecteur de ligands trace les liaisons hydrogène et va chercher un ligand 3D dans PubChem. En piquant deux atomes, on lit la distance en ångströms. Les « pilules » de résidus tapées dans la séquence projettent un halo 3D sur la structure.

Le mode Room View fait flotter la molécule dans votre vraie pièce, menu mural toujours opérationnel.

Prenons un cas simple : vous voulez inspecter une poche de liaison avant de lancer une campagne de docking. Sur écran plat, vous ouvrez PyMOL, vous chargez le PDB, vous tournez à la souris, vous mesurez des distances en ligne de commande. C'est efficace, mais abstrait.

Dans NexoPeek, vous chargez la même structure, vous la mettez à l'échelle, vous entrez littéralement dans la poche. La prédiction de poches PrankWeb / P2Rank allume le site druggable. Vous piquez deux atomes pour lire la distance en ångströms. Vous tapez un résidu dans la séquence et un halo 3D apparaît sur la structure. Ce n'est pas un remplacement de votre pipeline — c'est un outil de reconnaissance spatiale rapide, avant de revenir à vos scripts.

Le point technique intéressant, c'est que ce genre d'usage exige une latence faible et une image nette. Une poche de liaison fait quelques ångströms de large ; si le streaming bave, vous perdez la précision du geste. C'est exactement le problème que la bêta SteamVR adresse.

Étudiants en biotechnologie qui ont besoin de voir avant de mémoriser. Enseignants qui veulent montrer la glycolyse autrement qu'avec un schéma au tableau. Biologistes structuraux et cristallographes qui veulent inspecter une poche de liaison à l'échelle réelle. Professionnels de la découverte de médicaments qui cherchent un regard spatial rapide avant de lancer une campagne de docking.

NexoPeek est un logiciel éducatif et de visualisation scientifique. Ce n'est pas un dispositif médical, ni un avis médical, un diagnostic ou un traitement. Les aides à l'analyse — prédiction de poches, alignement — soutiennent le jugement professionnel, elles ne remplacent jamais les pipelines scientifiques validés.

Essayez NexoPeek sur Meta Quest : https://www.meta.com/experiences/nexopeek/1453797551140347/ — Step Inside the Molecule. Explore the Unseen World.

#9748. Hitting hCaptcha in 2026: What Developers Can Still Use

NoneCap is an hCaptcha solving API for developers: send a sitekey and page URL, get a token back. nonecap.com

NoneCap is an hCaptcha solving API for developers: send a sitekey and page URL, get a token back. nonecap.com

NoneCap is an hCaptcha solving API for developers: send a sitekey and page URL, get a token back. nonecap.com

If your scraper or test suite stopped at an hCaptcha widget sometime in the last two years, the service you used to send it to may be part of the problem.

2Captcha removed hCaptcha from its API documentation around the start of 2025. CapSolver's hCaptcha documentation page has returned a 404 since January 2025. If your code was written against either one for hCaptcha, you need a different place to send those jobs.

This post covers how token-based solving works, what to do when the site is yours, and one way to wire a solver into a script.

If the hCaptcha widget sits on an app you control and you only need your end-to-end tests to get past it, you don't need a solving service. hCaptcha publishes test keys for this. In your test environment, set the widget's sitekey to 10000000-ffff-ffff-ffff-000000000001 and your server's secret to the matching test secret from hCaptcha's docs. The widget then passes without a challenge and siteverify accepts the dummy token, so your CI never depends on a third party.

Everything below is for sites you don't control: a scraper collecting public data, a monitoring job, or a test that runs against a staging environment someone else owns.

When a person solves an hCaptcha, the widget gets back a token that starts with P1_. The page puts it in a hidden form field called h-captcha-response (or hands it to a JavaScript callback), and the site's backend checks it with hCaptcha's siteverify endpoint before it lets the request through.

A token-based solver gives you that same token without a browser on your side. The flow has four steps:

Two details trip people up. A token is single use and expires after about two minutes, so request it right before you submit, not at the start of a long job. And some sites check that the browser submitting the token matches the one that earned it, so send the User-Agent the solver returns with the token.

NoneCap is a hosted API that only handles hCaptcha, including invisible widgets and enterprise sitekeys that carry rqdata. You send a sitekey and a URL and get a token back. Failed solves aren't charged.

The wait parameter (1 to 90 seconds) holds the request open until the solve finishes. If it's still running when the window closes, you get a 202 with a null token, and you poll GET /v1/solves/{id} until the status is solved, failed or expired.

The same call from Node 18+, with no SDK:

In Playwright or Puppeteer, you'd read the sitekey from the page, make this call, write the token into the h-captcha-response textarea (plus the g-recaptcha-response compatibility field if the page has one), then submit the form or fire the widget's callback for invisible sitekeys.

One more thing helps over time. A token can pass hCaptcha and still be refused by the site that asked for it. When that happens, report the solve ID to POST /v1/feedback with "outcome": "rejected". It's the only way the service learns that a site turned a token down.

You may not need to rewrite anything. NoneCap has compatibility endpoints for both request formats:

The full API reference, with cURL and Go examples alongside the ones above, is at nonecap.com/api-reference. There are integration guides for Selenium, Playwright, Puppeteer, Scrapy and Go at nonecap.com/solutions, and a plain-text version of all the docs for coding assistants at nonecap.com/llms.txt.

NoneCap is an hCaptcha solving API for developers: send a sitekey and page URL, get a token back. nonecap.com

#9747. ToyBlocks: A controlled world for robot learning and evaluation

💻 Code | 📊 Data | 🤖 Models | 📖 Documentation

Robots are learning to fold laundry, sort parts, and handle unfamiliar objects. But those demonstrations are often rather narrow and don't explain what a robot has learned or why it fails.

To study a complex system, scientists often begin with a small, controlled environment, such as a petri dish or terrarium, where they can vary conditions and observe the effects. Robotics needs environments that make this kind of investigation possible—researchers should be able to change the training data or model design, repeat a test, and trace the cause of a failure.

Today we're introducing a framework for creating these environments; we call them FoundationWorlds. Each pairs a controlled, simulated world targeted at studying robotics in a specific environment with tools for automatically generating tasks and training demonstrations, as well as metrics for measuring a robot's behavior over time. Together, they provide a setting for studying questions such as how models improve as more training data becomes available, and how to best combine high-level reasoning with precise physical control.

Our first foundation world is ToyBlocks: an open simulation framework built around a robot arm and blocks on a tabletop. The setting is deliberately simple, but the robot must still reason about how the blocks interact and how to arrange them while pushing, flipping, and stacking.

ToyBlocks automatically generates demonstrations, which are recordings of a robot completing tasks in simulation, without requiring time-consuming teleoperation, in which a person remotely controls the robot. Researchers can easily vary these training experiences. For example, a team could generate more pushing or flipping demonstrations, then evaluate performance on tasks kept out of training.

Starting with ToyBlocks as our first FoundationWorld, we aim to extend the approach to increasingly complex environments.

Building on our earlier work in open robot learning, including MolmoAct 2, MolmoBot, and MolmoSpaces, ToyBlocks gives researchers a way to study robotics questions in a deliberately constrained domain.

As a FoundationWorld, ToyBlocks is designed around four requirements: (1) realistic physics and appearance, (2) automatic generation of tasks and demonstrations at scale, (3) challenges that combine reasoning with dexterity, and (4) broad coverage of the tasks possible within a domain.

Open-ended domains require modeling a wide range of objects and interactions, making it infeasible to fulfill all these requirements. ToyBlocks’ narrow scope, on the other hand, makes it possible to fulfill them all.

Within ToyBlocks' smaller setting, researchers can work toward investigating how a robot can learn to perform any reasonable task while being confident that the simulated arm and blocks behave very similarly to their physical counterparts.

A physical robot gripper above wooden blocks in the ToyBlocks setup.

ToyBlocks is not just about picking and stacking blocks: pictures and letters on the blocks' faces allow for searching, sorting, and arranging tasks. A robot may need to turn a block to see a hidden face before deciding where it belongs. Domain randomization – varying block size, table height, and other physical properties from scene to scene – tests how well models generalize as the geometry changes.

ToyBlocks automatically generates skills (behaviors for short tasks) and task demonstrations that can be used to train models or adapt previously trained models through additional training (fine-tuning). High-level reasoning models decide what to do; low-level action models control the robot’s movements. The framework can also be used to easily design experiments and validate hypotheses.

ToyBlocks uses reinforcement learning (RL) and motion planning, which computes how the robot should move, to generate skills for short-horizon tasks, which involve brief sequences of actions. Skill training takes place in Isaac Lab, Nvidia's open-source framework for robot learning in simulation. Through trial and error, these policies – models that choose the robot’s actions – learn non-prehensile skills such as pushing a block across the table or flipping it onto another face without picking it up. Skill generation can draw on privileged information – values the simulator can supply directly but a real robot cannot, such as a block's exact position and orientation – instead of estimating it from camera images. This enables the automatic generation of skills that would require teleoperation in the real world.

To generate demonstration data, a task-and-motion planner (TAMP) automatically selects and sequences the skills needed to solve a task and plans the robot’s movements between them. Running each plan in simulation produces a dataset of recorded demonstrations along with labels describing which task or skill the robot performs. ToyBlocks scales data generation through generating and executing hundreds of such plans in parallel on a single graphics processing unit (GPU), reaching up to 24 times real-time performance.

Acting from sensor observations adds a perception problem: a model has to estimate a block’s pose – its position and orientation – which the simulator could supply directly. To reflect real-world conditions, ToyBlocks trains models that map raw sensor observations to actions.

Execution of Molmo 2 (a high-level model) and ManiFlow (a low-level model) trained in ToyBlocks. Molmo 2 selects skills such as rotation and flipping, indicating the relevant block via a pointing interface, while ManiFlow controls the simulated arm to execute the commanded skills.

ToyBlocks' controllable data generator lets users create training mixtures that emphasize particular skills or fill gaps in existing datasets. Researchers can study how much data a model needs and which experiences help it generalize to unseen tasks. For example, they could test whether adding rotation and pick-and-place demonstrations improves flipping, or vary the balance of examples inside and outside a defined workspace region—evaluating their choices on tasks kept out of training. Importantly, evaluation of trained models generates metrics beyond success rates; it provides information such as execution speeds, forces exerted on objects, and task progress measured via the same specifications used by the planning module.

A webpage interface lets users connect Claude – or another frontier model – and use natural language to instruct the robot or try tasks, offering a way to explore how a model plans and acts without needing robotics expertise.

The evaluations below use ToyBlocks to study how training data and methods affect performance, spatial reasoning, generalization to new letters and block appearances, multi-step planning, transfer to physical robots, and frontier models that act through tools. Users can easily design their own tasks and measures to investigate other questions—for example, whether a model performs better when it selects objects by pointing or by issuing text commands such as "pick the yellow block."

Low-level action models, such as vision-language-action models (VLAs), map language instructions and visual observations to robot actions.

The premise of VLAs is that, by pretraining on large-scale datasets, they can rapidly generalize to different scenarios or a specific workspace. However, evidence on how well these action models generalize remains conflicting. Some studies report that these action models are brittle to changes in inputs, such as different object layouts and lighting, whereas others show that VLAs generalize well. We argue that these studies often rely on real-world datasets with limited flexibility in spatial variations. ToyBlocks enables us to test how well action models generalize in a simple, easily reproducible setting with meaningful task-space diversity.

We design generalization tests that vary the skill sequences needed to complete an instruction, the letters or colors on the blocks, and the number of blocks in a scene. A stacking study can withhold four-block stacks from training, then test whether a model can combine familiar movements to build them. Workspace studies distinguish performance at new positions within a training region from performance beyond its boundaries, where the model has to extrapolate. We illustrate the study setup and findings below.

We consider four tasks: Stack, Unstack, Flip, and Rotate. For these tasks, we study interpolation (new configurations within the training range) and extrapolation (configurations beyond that range). For example, we evaluate generalization by training on scenarios where objects spawn only in the left region (green) and testing on the right region (orange), or by training on stack heights of 2 and 5 blocks and testing on heights 3 and 4.

Spatial generalization studies for VLA models (results based on ManiFlow, π0.5, and MolmoAct 2). Despite large-scale pretraining, these popular action models generalize poorly in the initial results. We improve generalization and analyze the contribution of each technique. The chart’s LoRA label stands for low-rank adaptation, a method for fine-tuning a model with a small set of trainable weight updates. We believe action model generalization remains far from solved; ToyBlocks provides a valuable testbed for systematically exploring generalization techniques.

Long-horizon tasks, which require many steps, allow us to measure how well models can plan a sequence of actions to solve them. Our framework enables us to create such long-horizon tasks, and create oracles – reference components that provide correct plans or actions – at both the high and low levels. This allows us to isolate whether the high-level planning or low-level execution failed when a model fails at a task. An example long-horizon task might be to spell “Ai2” with a block stack; because the letters may not be immediately visible, the agent must first choose actions that reveal information, and then plan and execute a sequence of actions to build the stack.

We evaluate hierarchical models with explicit high-level planning and low-level execution models. In this instance, we choose Molmo 2, a vision-language model (VLM), as the high-level planner, and ManiFlow as the low-level policy. Molmo 2 chooses the skill to execute and the block to execute it on, while the low-level model executes the instruction. We train low-level models such as ManiFlow to pause after completing the execution and query the high-level model for the next instruction. We evaluate the model’s planning abilities on three scenarios of increasing difficulty. The easiest scenario initializes with each character upright and facing the camera. The medium scenario has characters that may not be upright, and the hardest scenario contains characters that are not visible at the start of the episode.

Success rates on three-letter block-spelling tasks using Molmo 2 as the high-level reasoning model and either ManiFlow or a motion planner for low-level manipulation. An example task is “Stack Ai2”. Molmo 2 and ManiFlow are trained on ToyBlocks and evaluated across three difficulty settings and two generalization conditions.

Our experiments with agentic systems test how frontier models plan and act through tool calls. We study three settings using Claude Opus 5.5. In the search-and-spell setting, we expose ToyBlocks skills through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), a standard for connecting AI applications to tools. The agent sees the scene through camera images, calls skills such as pick, flip, or rotate by pointing at a pixel, and decides when to search, build, or declare the task complete or impossible. The same MCP tools can execute either the scripted skills that generate ToyBlocks demonstrations (motion-planned pick and place, plus RL-based rotate and flip) or learned ManiFlow skills. ToyBlocks includes the framework behind these experiments, which also powers the natural-language web interface described earlier.

A frontier model (Claude Fable 5.1) controls a robot in a ToyBlocks world to search for and stack blocks into a tower spelling “Ai2.” During the episode, the agent muses, “I need to figure out whether pick-and-place naturally straightens orientation or if I need to correct it manually… I have 63 calls left, plenty to run a controlled test” (0:06). The agent later hypothesizes: “…maybe the gripper’s yaw is radial—pointing from the robot base toward the block” (0:15) and eventually confirms this hypothesis (0:26) before constructing the three-block tower, but the ‘A’ is sideways (1:11). Surprisingly, current frontier models often make similar perceptual errors (see the next figure), despite their impressive planning, spatial reasoning, and search capabilities.

For classical planning, the agent (our system using Claude Opus 5.5 to plan and choose actions) solves all 30 of a group of block-stacking tasks similar to ones that frontier models struggled with a few years ago, using text descriptions. It also solves 30 out of 30 while repeatedly observing camera images and choosing its next action in a closed loop.

In the search-and-spell setting, the agent had to generate stacks spelling out three-letter words. It had to find the blocks with the corresponding letters among up to eight blocks in the scene. Importantly, 50% of the scenes did not have blocks with all the required letters, rendering the task infeasible. In this case, we required the agent to state that the task is infeasible. We found that in this experiment, the agent was able to successfully solve or correctly declare infeasible 63% of the tasks. Errors were mostly caused by the agent confusing letters with look-alike letters (13%) or choosing an incorrect orientation for a letter in a stack (15%).

Our results also show that the agent was able to solve the task more efficiently when the blocks had semantic regularities, or patterns, taking advantage of such patterns to reason about occluded faces. For instance, in most of the infeasible scenes, when the blocks had no patterns, the agent correctly looked at all the blocks’ faces before declaring infeasibility, whereas it was able to declare infeasibility significantly faster when the blocks had semantic patterns.

Our third experimental setting asks whether an agent can learn how its skills behave, using experiments as a scientist would. When a skill behaves unexpectedly, the agent forms a hypothesis, designs a small test, and revises its understanding from the result. We expand on this idea by having an agent run its own experiments and write its own skill descriptions based on what it finds. These learned descriptions raise success rates from 24% with the default descriptions to 63%, outperforming the 36% achieved with descriptions written by a human expert.

Share of letter-block faces the agent had exposed by the end of each “search and spell” episode (bars averaged over 20 episodes; one marker per episode, styled by outcome). In a feasible task every letter of the three-letter target word is present; in an infeasible task, one letter is missing and the agent should say so. Each patterned block carries uppercase and lowercase instances of a letter, plus images that begin with the letter (e.g., A-block: apple, ant, A, 1, airplane, a); an unpatterned block’s six faces are randomized and unrelated. Correct: the tower spelled the word, or for infeasible tasks, the agent correctly declared the task impossible. Letter rotated or look-alike: the agent built the tower, but a letter was turned or a look-alike substituted, including five infeasible tasks declared solved with a look-alike in the missing letter’s place. Block fell out of reach; reported: a needed block was pushed out of the arm’s reach, so the agent reported that its task had become impossible. No report: the agent used up its motor-skill budget and stopped without claiming either outcome. With patterned blocks, the agent finishes having seen fewer faces, because it can infer what hidden faces must depict rather than checking every one.

Action-conditioned world models are trained to predict how a scene changes in response to a robot’s actions. Using them as an alternative to model-based simulators for training and evaluating robot policies is an active area of research. How well they serve this purpose depends on how accurately they predict physical interactions, which is hard to measure without knowing the true state of the scene. ToyBlocks provides this ground truth – the actual simulated scene state – enabling highly controlled tests of how recently developed world models perform in low-level object manipulation. Here, the arm’s end effector is its gripper.

Specifically, we tested whether action-conditioned world models are capable of predicting the motions of blocks or the outcomes of skill executions after being trained on example executions. To do so, we chose four different skills (pick-and-place, flip, rotate, and a mixed task) and generated 900 trajectories – sequences of robot states and actions over time – for each skill. 50% of these trajectories were successful demonstrations of the skill, and 50% were unsuccessful because of small changes to spatial configurations. With equal numbers of successful and unsuccessful executions, a model that always predicts success would be correct only half the time. The models were fine-tuned on these demonstrations and then tested on their ability to predict the outcome of action sequences of the same skills.

We find that Wan 2.2 predicts block motion and task outcomes most accurately. Astra tracks the gripper well but struggles to simulate contact. LeWM is fast and more accurate over short interaction segments, though it drifts over full trajectories. In additional experiments, we also showed that models that score higher on pose and success prediction also produce better training data: adding 100 model-generated trajectories (rollouts) from the best video-generation model raises a policy’s success in an unseen region from 19% to 78%.

We tested three types of models: a video prediction model with 5 billion parameters (Wan 2.2), an agentic model that created its own physics simulator tuned to match the demonstration data (Astra), and a latent world model (LeWM). During testing, each trained model has to predict future images, simulator states, or latent states (learned internal representations), respectively, based on an initial image and a sequence of actions. For full trajectories, models use the initial image as the only observed image, along with the action sequence. For short interaction segments – a single pick, place, flip, or rotate – models start from the real image immediately before that interaction. Full trajectories show how errors accumulate over long horizons, while interaction segments isolate a single interaction, such as the gripper making contact with a block, and show how well the model predicts it. To compare models fairly, we probe each model’s predictions, reading out where it expects the blocks and gripper to be at different points in the trajectory and whether it expects the task to succeed at the end.

Sim-to-real evaluations test policies trained in simulation on physical robots performing block manipulation tasks. By comparing simulation and real-world execution, we assess whether behaviors and failure patterns observed in simulation provide meaningful indications of real-world performance. For example, researchers can evaluate individual skills and their composition in longer-horizon tasks to identify where failures arise and whether these patterns carry over to physical deployments.

We test whether the models trained entirely on ToyBlocks simulation datasets can be deployed in the real world zero-shot, without training on real-world examples. We evaluate ManiFlow and each low-level skill (pick, place, flip, and rotate) individually. We test whether the hierarchical system (Molmo 2 + ManiFlow) can complete long-horizon three-block spelling tasks requiring sequences of these actions. Real-world experiments use a Franka FR3 arm with a Robotiq gripper across thirty scene configurations. Each scene contains 4–10 blocks seen during training. An episode is successful only if the relevant blocks are moved to target poses without collisions. If the operator intervenes to stop the robot due to an unsafe motion during an episode, it is marked as a failure.

ManiFlow’s atomic-skill success rates were similar in simulation and the real world (80.0% and 81.1%). The hierarchical Molmo 2 + ManiFlow system succeeded in 55.5% of simulated episodes (111/200) and 50.0% of real-world episodes (15/30); further trials are needed to establish statistical confidence across tasks.

Success rates of the ManiFlow low-level model and the hierarchical Molmo 2–ManiFlow system in simulation and the real world. For ManiFlow, the total count represents individual skill executions (pick, place, flip, and rotate), whereas for Molmo 2–ManiFlow, it represents block-spelling task episodes. The Molmo 2–ManiFlow evaluations use the easiest scene configuration defined in the simulation evaluation, with block characters visible and upright.

Side-by-side real-world and simulated block-stacking executions using the same high-level planner. Pink rings mark the planner’s target point for each skill. The scenes use different block labels, and simulation playback is retimed to align grasps and releases with the real robot.

To transfer Molmo 2 and ManiFlow – both trained exclusively on ToyBlocks data – to a physical robot, we address the differences between simulation and reality in three stages.

Before data generation, we perform system identification by tuning simulated robot parameters, including joint friction and armature (the motor and gearbox inertia reflected at the joint), to match real-robot trajectories. During data generation, we randomize physical properties (object size, friction, and table height) and visual properties (lighting, backgrounds, materials, and camera parameters). At inference time, observations are captured using a front-facing ZED camera and a wrist-mounted ZED Mini. For policies that use depth images, we generate clean depth maps, which estimate distance at each pixel, from paired red-green-blue (RGB) camera images using FastFoundationStereo, rather than relying on noisy depth sensor measurements.

The physical ToyBlocks setup: a robot arm, wooden blocks, and a camera.

ToyBlocks connects data generation, training, and evaluation in one controlled setting, so researchers can investigate how robots learn over time and test how changes to a model or its training data affect robot behavior. We’re releasing simulation assets, procedural task and demonstration generators, automatically generated demonstrations, two trained models showcasing what the framework can do (one based on Molmo 2 and one based on ManiFlow), training code, and evaluation code and validation sets. This allows other teams to build their own training mixtures and investigate failure modes beyond those covered in our initial experiments.

Our initial data release is a proof point with 85,336 long-horizon demonstrations, each comprising about 6–12 skill demonstrations, depending on the set. The initial datasets cover nearly 1,600 hours of robot execution data and 144 million frames. In a few weeks, we're targeting a second release with a larger-scale dataset, more skills, and more comprehensive benchmarking. We’ll also add fully integrated RL training capability that is not contained in the current package.

Other directions for ToyBlocks include bimanual (two-arm) manipulation and dexterous robot hands, equipped with force and touch sensors for studying motion and tasks that involve frequent physical contact. We're also exploring play with unstructured piles of blocks as a way to collect data and study how new behaviors and tasks might emerge through interaction.

Future direction: RL-based pile manipulation.

Future direction: bimanual block manipulation.

With ToyBlocks, we want to advance the science of robot learning toward a future where robots can reliably apply what they've learned to unfamiliar tasks and environments. We encourage the research community to explore ToyBlocks for their own investigations and even as a basis to build their own FoundationWorlds.

#9745. Only the Design of a Local LLM Eval Harness Survives — Rebuilding It for Qwen3.8 27B

Posted on Nov 9 • Originally published at wada-dev.com

Three weeks ago, to settle whether Ornith 1.0 35B (MoE 35B/A3B) deserved to be opencode's default on my RTX 5090, I wrote a harness that makes a model port RFC 6902 (JSON Patch) to Rust (The 3x faster local LLM that couldn't finish the job). It was three times faster and matched on quality for one-shot work, but went 0-5 on multi-step agent tasks, and Ornith ended up demoted to a speed lane.

Qwen3.8 27B came out, so I ran it through the same harness. I switched: the default moved from Qwen3.6 27B to Qwen3.8 27B.

But that isn't what I want to write about. What I want to write about is that what survived was not the script but the design. The script itself lived in /tmp, and /tmp was gone.

Last time's lesson fits on one line. One-shot accuracy does not predict multi-step completion. A model that looks fast and capable on a single answer drops its state on the fifth turn. Going 0-5 taught me that properly.

So published benchmark numbers are only a starting point. I looked at the official figures this time too, and they were good. But that decides "worth trying", not "make it the default". The second question can only be answered by whether it gets through my own task.

It isn't a benchmark — it's actual porting work. Port RFC 6902 and RFC 6901 from the Python reference implementation to Rust. Pass or fail is decided solely by the official conformance suite: 112 cases, 4 of them disabled. That's split into four phases, run one phase per session, with the model unloaded between phases so nothing carries over. The phase split (test runner → JSON Pointer → add/remove/replace → move/copy/test) is unchanged from the previous post.

What makes the design work is not how it measures performance but how it prevents cheating.

The suite and the reference implementation are read-only. chmod a-w, and after the run I diff -r them against the originals. That closes the path of loosening a test to go green.

The model's words don't count as evidence. The verdict always comes from me running cargo test. Last time I watched a model deliver a correct fix and then explain, at length, a function that did not exist — so this one is non-negotiable.

One phase has "must be red" as its done condition. The first phase is a stub implementation, so red is correct. If a model reports green there, that report is itself the evidence of cheating. It's a tripwire.

First-attempt passes are recorded in a separate column from passes-with-retries. That's new this time. A model that goes red and then succeeds when a human says "try again" is costing me something real, and I don't want that mixed into the same "passed".

Qwen3.6 got through this task in July. That's why it held the default. But back then I wasn't separating first-attempt from retried passes, so it can't be lined up rigorously against this round's numbers.

All three green on the first attempt, no retries, tamper check clean.

More convincing than the numbers: all three reached exactly pass=88 fail=20 at the third phase. 88 of 112 done, the remaining 20 belonging to the next phase — the same breakdown three times over. That isn't luck, it's a stable route into the problem. That's where the decision got made.

Worth recording the times my own read was wrong. Half the value of a harness is here.

First, VRAM. Qwen3.8 has a hybrid attention stack with full attention on only one layer in four, so I wrote in a config comment that the KV cache would shrink and it would sit lighter than Qwen3.6. Measured: 29.2GB. Heavier than the 26.7GB recorded for Qwen3.6 back in late June. The measurement conditions weren't perfectly matched, but either way it did not get lighter.

I assume the vision tower and the per-layer recurrent state on the linear-attention side are what cost the difference, but I never isolated them. All I measured was the total; the cause is speculation. What I know is that the prediction was wrong. The comment did say "not yet measured, check after deploy", so I rewrote it — prediction included — once the number came in. I had also written "this is now the tightest fit on the box", which was simply false: eight lines below sits another model at 31.8GB. I hadn't read my own table.

Second, speed. After upgrading the runtime and moving from an unofficial GGUF to the official tag, one-shot generation went from 72 tok/s to 143 tok/s. I changed the runtime version and the model artifact at the same time, so I can't separate them, but given that the newer runtime is the one with a native linear-attention implementation, I'd guess that's the main cause.

Either way it doubled. I assumed multi-step work would speed up too. It didn't. Each run took 1161-1879 seconds. Obvious in hindsight: what dominates multi-step wall-clock isn't token generation, it's the round trips — read and write files, run the tests, read the output, decide what's next. Doubling generation doesn't even get you 1.5x overall.

Everything I'd mentally credited to that tok/s number had to be written back down. The reason to switch wasn't speed, it was the first-attempt pass rate.

As I said up top, the old harness kept its inputs in /tmp, and /tmp was wiped. Only the output side survived.

Rebuilding still took minutes. The conformance suite is officially distributed and the reference implementation is public. The plan file and the agent instructions were still in the experiment directory. Everything needed to reproduce it was written down somewhere.

The part that mattered most: the plan file recorded the counts — "tests.json has 95 cases, spec_tests.json has 17, 112 total, 4 disabled". Count the files you fetched, match the numbers, and you know you didn't grab the wrong thing. I originally wrote that line as a pass condition ("a runner that loads fewer than 112 cases is broken"). Using it to validate the inputs themselves never occurred to me.

So "I reused the same script" isn't accurate. What I reused was the design; the script was rewritten. The counting rule changed too. What survived was the phase split, the machine-only-verdict principle, the anti-cheat construction, and the count invariant. Because those were in a document, losing the artifact cost almost nothing.

Honestly, this measures one task family. Porting from Python to Rust is a fairly specific shape. How it handles images, the quality of its Japanese, whether it can actually recall something after 200K tokens — all outside this harness.

So I think it's enough to justify swapping the default, but not enough to justify deleting every other model. Qwen3.6 is still there.

And when the next model shows up, this round's script has probably vanished too. That's fine. What I can't afford to lose isn't the artifact — it's why I chose to measure that way.

#9744. TurnWise Outperforms Streaming Video RL Baselines Across Three Benchmarks

Among other things, launching AIModels.fyi ... Find the right AI model for your project - https://aimodels.fyi

Among other things, launching AIModels.fyi ... Find the right AI model for your project - https://aimodels.fyi

Among other things, launching AIModels.fyi ... Find the right AI model for your project - https://aimodels.fyi

TurnWise applies turn-level Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to streaming video, where a model repeatedly chooses to answer or wait as new frames arrive. Its central claim is specific: silence-completed prefix scoring estimates each decision’s group-relative remaining return, so a later reply is not trained using rewards earned before that decision.

The problem is that standard trajectory-level GRPO broadcasts one advantage across every turn. A redundant reply after an early success can inherit positive credit, while a useful follow-up after earlier failures can inherit negative credit. TurnWise separates the return from each turn onward from the reward already accrued, then weights response and waiting turns equally in the policy loss.

The method is evaluated on ProactiveVQA, OVO-Timing, and StreamingBench using Qwen2.5-VL-3B and Qwen3-VL-4B backbones. The authors report the best aggregate scores on all three benchmarks with both models, and say that turn-mean aggregation improves response timing while reducing repetition relative to credit-only optimization. A related video-RL direction emphasizes focused video reasoning, whereas TurnWise focuses on when to respond during a stream.

Streaming interaction differs from offline video question answering because the model acts on partial observations and must account for what it has already told the user. A response can be timely and useful at one point, while another response at a later decision adds no information. The learning signal therefore needs to reflect both answer quality and the timing of each response-or-wait choice.

The paper positions TurnWise against MMDuet2, ThinkStream, and StreamPro, which improve interaction rewards or assess response-level and trajectory-level quality. It argues that these reward designs still leave a key GRPO issue: a single trajectory advantage is shared across turns. TurnWise changes credit assignment and loss weighting rather than introducing a new trajectory reward. The broader distinction between shared sequence feedback and per-step credit also appears in turn-level credit assignment, although TurnWise applies it to streaming video response and waiting decisions.

The concrete failure case is a trajectory with a successful early answer followed by a redundant reply: the later action may still receive positive shared credit. The reverse can happen when a useful follow-up follows earlier failures. The authors’ correction subtracts group-relative accrued reward before each decision, allowing later turns to be judged by their remaining return.

Illustrative dialogue and advantage plot contrasting shared GRPO credit with TurnWise credit across turns.

The example contrasts a shared trajectory advantage with TurnWise’s remaining-return credit, showing how a later redundant reply can inherit earlier success under GRPO. The distinction motivates turn-specific learning signals.

For each sampled trajectory, TurnWise keeps the first t actions and replaces every later action with silence, then scores that prefix with the same observation plan and evaluation horizon. The difference between this score and the full trajectory score gives the return from turn t onward. Group-relative normalization produces a turn-specific advantage without a learned critic. The remaining-return construction is related in granularity to Turn-PPO advantage estimation, but TurnWise derives its signal from silence-completed video prefixes.

The prefix scores reuse the existing trajectory evaluations: the authors state that a silent suffix changes neither retained responses nor their preceding replies. This avoids additional rollouts and judge calls. A limitation of the method’s credit signal is that it depends on the fixed trajectory scorer, including its response-quality, timing, repetition, and out-of-window penalties.

TurnWise also changes the GRPO objective. It averages token losses within each turn and then averages across turns, so a long textual answer does not outweigh a short waiting action merely because it contains more tokens. The two mechanisms address separate issues: remaining-return advantages determine what credit a turn receives, while turn-mean aggregation determines how much that turn contributes to optimization.

TurnWise pipeline from streaming inputs and sampled trajectories to turn advantages and turn-mean loss.

The overview connects silence-completed prefix scoring to group-relative remaining-return advantages, then applies turn-mean aggregation. It summarizes how TurnWise aligns credit and policy weighting with streaming decisions.

Training starts from supervised fine-tuning on 100,874 instruction examples, then uses 3,983 streaming instances with groups of four sampled trajectories. The reward is PAUC-based and judged by gpt-oss-20b; the evaluation covers proactive answer quality, event-triggered timing, and real-time visual understanding. The paper reports one epoch of RL training for each configuration.

The named RL comparisons are MMDuet2, ThinkStream, and StreamPro, implemented in the same streaming GRPO framework, alongside the supervised models. TurnWise achieves the best aggregate scores on ProactiveVQA, OVO-Timing, and StreamingBench for both Qwen backbones. The supplied paper text does not include the numerical benchmark scores, so the size of its gains cannot be quantified here. A related line of work also studies turn-level credit policy optimization, while the comparisons reported here are MMDuet2, ThinkStream, and StreamPro.

The authors also report a component-level result: turn-mean aggregation improves response timing and reduces repetition compared with credit-only optimization. This supports their claim that turn-specific credit alone does not fix length-dependent weighting. The paper text provided does not specify a numerical repetition reduction or timing improvement.

TurnWise’s technical contribution is the pairing of silence-completed prefix scoring with turn-mean policy optimization. The first removes earlier accrued reward from a decision’s group-relative signal; the second gives each sampled response-or-wait decision equal loss weight. Both operate within GRPO and use the existing rollout group rather than a critic or extra trajectories.

The reported evidence is broad across three streaming benchmarks and two Qwen backbones, but the supplied results section gives aggregate rankings rather than score tables. It also does not provide the numerical gains, per-category results, or detailed ablation values. Those omissions limit how precisely a reader can compare effect sizes from the available text.

The paper’s stated edge case is the mismatch between trajectory quality and individual turn quality: a good trajectory can contain a bad turn, and a poor trajectory can contain a useful one. TurnWise is designed to address that mismatch under the paper’s PAUC-based scorer and streaming setup. Its reported findings do not establish performance beyond the listed benchmarks and configurations. Unlike difficulty-aware video RL, which targets video generation, TurnWise evaluates streaming video understanding and interaction timing.

This is a Plain English Papers summary of a research paper called Turns Matter: Advancing Streaming Video RL via Turn-Level Credit.
