#9743. Your Experts Have Partners. There's HOPE for Keeping Them Together

Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have enabled state-of-the-art LLMs to be scaled to hundreds of billions of parameters, but they come with a fundamental and costly caveat: every expert MLP must occupy memory at inference time, even though the vast majority are idle for any given token. For example, Qwen3.5-122B has 256 experts in each of its 48 MoE layers, and 95% of its ~250 GB parameter memory footprint is taken up entirely by these expert MLPs alone. However, for any given token, only 8 experts in each layer are actually used.

Expert pruning is one of the most direct fixes to this memory bottleneck. That is, permanently delete the least useful experts. Pruning avoids the latency issues which make dynamic loading/off-loading of experts impractical; it does not require any training; and it composes with quantization. Given these attractive benefits and the simplicity of the idea, it's easy to see why expert pruning has become a go-to approach for shrinking MoEs. The difficulty lies in deciding which experts are safest to remove.

Existing pruning methods score each expert independently, assigning every expert a scalar importance score (based on a calibration dataset), and cutting out the least important experts (in each layer independently). These are first-order methods, because they assume each expert's contribution is independent of all others. In reality, experts form cooperative groups. We observe consistent clusters of co-activated experts in our own experiments, and independent work has shown that expert cooperation is a stable property of MoEs and is important for model performance. Ignoring these interactions leads to suboptimal pruning, especially at aggressive rates.

Our newest paper derives HOPE (Higher-Order Pruning of Experts), a second-order method that accounts for pairwise expert interactions. At 50% pruning, HOPE achieves the best average rank of any method, with gains of up to +6.1% on agentic coding tasks over the next-best pruning method.

In this post, we explain how HOPE works, show where it outperforms existing methods, and walk through how to use it for your own models. For readers unfamiliar with MoE architectures, see Mixture of Experts (MoEs) in Transformers.

In a standard MoE, each layer has EEE experts, and each input token xxx is routed independently to KKK such experts ( K=8 K = 8 K=8 is a typical choice). Routing is performed by a single layer which produces softmax-normalized gate weights gk(x)g_{k}(x)gk​(x) for each expert kkk, wherein the KKK experts with the highest gate weights are selected to form the active set of experts, T(x)⊂{1,..,E}T(x) \subset\{1,..,E\}T(x)⊂{1,..,E}. The output of the layer is then ∑k∈T(x)gk(x)fk(x)\sum\limits_{k\in T(x)}g_{k}(x)f_{k}(x)k∈T(x)∑​gk​(x)fk​(x), where fk(x)f_{k}(x)fk​(x) is the output of expert kkk for token xxx.

Left: typical MoE layer, where each token is routed to the top-K experts. Right: first-order methods rank and delete experts based on a scalar importance score, but the best pruning decisions will also consider the strength of interactions between experts.

Importantly, experts in the selected set T(x)T(x)T(x) are not independent. Experts form stable cooperative groups that get consistently co-activated together. This has been observed before in the literature, as well: expert co-selection patterns emerge early in training and stabilize throughout.

This means that when we prune experts from an MoE layer, pruning decisions need to consider the higher-order effects between these experts. Removing expert A might seem fine on its own, but if expert B—which frequently cooperates with and relies on A—is highly important, then removing A would dismantle a cooperative group just through a single deletion. First-order methods miss this entirely, because they score A and B separately.

This effect compounds at high pruning rates. When we remove up to 50% of experts, we risk breaking many cooperative links. This is where second-order pruning is most advantageous.

(See Appendix A in our corresponding paper for the full derivation of the HOPE objective)

When we delete a set of PPP experts from some MoE layer, the selected set of experts T(x)T(x)T(x) (for any token xxx) can change. The pruned experts that would have been selected are replaced by the experts with the next-highest gate weights. The resulting change in layer output is the pruning error. Our goal is to find the prune-set PPP (of some predefined pruning budget ∣P∣\vert P\vert∣P∣) that minimizes the resulting pruning error (over tokens xxx from our calibration set).

Unfortunately, minimizing the pruning error over PPP directly is intractable. The pruning error depends on the identities of the replacement experts, which in turn depend on the prune-set PPP itself. HOPE sidesteps this by defining a tractable surrogate ZZZ, which strictly upper-bounds the dominant component of the pruning error:

Z=[∑j∈P∩T(x)gj(x)∥fj(x)∥2]2≥true errorZ = \bigl[\sum\limits_{j \in P\cap T(x)} g_{j}(x)\Vert f_j(x)\Vert_{2}\bigr]^{2} \geq \text{true error}Z=[j∈P∩T(x)∑​gj​(x)∥fj​(x)∥2​]2≥true error

Because ZZZ is a squared sum, expanding it naturally produces cross-terms gi(x)gj(x)∥fi(x)∥2∥fj(x)∥2g_{i}(x)g_{j}(x)\Vert f_{i}(x)\Vert_{2}\Vert f_{j}(x)\Vert_{2}gi​(x)gj​(x)∥fi​(x)∥2​∥fj​(x)∥2​ between pairs of experts. These are the interaction terms that first-order methods discard.

To find the optimal prune-set, HOPE minimizes E[Z]\mathbb{E}[Z]E[Z] over the calibration set, which can be reformulated as the following quadratic program:

P∗=arg min⁡p  p⊤Fps.t.p∈{0,1}E,∑k=1Epk=∣P∣P^{*} = \argmin_{p}\; p^{\top}Fp \quad \text{s.t.} \quad p \in \{0,1\}^{E}, \sum\limits_{k=1}^{E}p_{k} = \vert P\vertP∗=pargmin​p⊤Fps.t.p∈{0,1}E,k=1∑E​pk​=∣P∣

where F∈RE×EF\in\mathbb{R}^{E\times E}F∈RE×E is defined as:

Fi,j=1∣Xi,j∣∑x∈Xi,jgi(x)gj(x)∥fi(x)∥2∥fj(x)∥2whereXi,j={x:i,j∈T(x)}F_{i,j} = \frac{1}{\vert \mathcal{X}_{i,j}\vert} \sum\limits_{x\in\mathcal{X}_{i,j}} g_{i}(x)g_{j}(x)\Vert f_{i}(x)\Vert_{2}\Vert f_{j}(x)\Vert_{2}\quad\text{where}\quad \mathcal{X}_{i,j} = \{x: i,j \in T(x)\}Fi,j​=∣Xi,j​∣1​x∈Xi,j​∑​gi​(x)gj​(x)∥fi​(x)∥2​∥fj​(x)∥2​whereXi,j​={x:i,j∈T(x)}

This F-matrix is collected on the calibration dataset, and the optimal prune-set is obtained by solving the resulting quadratic program (QP) with a continuous relaxation (then rounding to binary solutions). Each entry Fi,jF_{i,j}Fi,j​ captures the average gate-weighted output product of experts iii and jjj, across tokens where both are co-activated. Whereas the diagonal Fk,kF_{k,k}Fk,k​ measures individual expert importance, the off-diagonal entries ( Fi,jF_{i,j}Fi,j​ for i≠ji\neq ji=j) measure pairwise cooperative contribution.

What does FFF look like in practice? It shows the structure of expert cooperation, which depends on layer:

Visualization of the interaction matrix F for GLM-4.5-Air (128 experts per layer, 106B parameters total) at three representative layers (early, middle, late). Experts have been clustered to reveal block structure. Bright blocks along the diagonal indicate groups of experts with strong pairwise interaction scores.

In terms of practical cost, HOPE requires the same calibration pass as any other expert-pruning method (one forward pass over calibration data). The only addition is solving the quadratic program, which is non-convex, but can be solved efficiently via a standard QP solver (1–2 seconds each layer). The total additional overhead is negligible compared to first-order methods, as the time for calibration dominates.

Notably, HOPE has a strong connection to Router-weighted Expert Activation Pruning (REAP), a state-of-the-art first-order expert-pruning method. HOPE's F-matrix encodes individual expert importance scores on the diagonal, and this diagonal effectively recovers the scores used by REAP to independently rank experts for pruning (differing only by the variance of expert contributions). The diagonal of FFF recovers REAP's expert rankings almost perfectly (Spearman ρ=0.988\rho = 0.988ρ=0.988). Thus, any improvement HOPE achieves over REAP is attributable to the second-order interaction terms in the off-diagonal entries of the FFF-matrix.

We evaluated HOPE as an expert pruning method using 3 models (Qwen3.5-122B, Qwen3.5-35B, and GLM-4.5-Air), with 2 calibration datasets (Evol-CodeAlpaca and SWE-Bench Verified trajectories). We used the Tulu3 suite and SWE-Bench Pro (agentic coding) to test the resulting pruned models, comparing HOPE to 4 first-order baselines (REAP, MAN, EAN, and Frequency) across pruning rates spanning from 10% to 50%.

HOPE achieves the best overall rank across conditions and dominates at aggressive pruning rates. Left: average rank (lower = better) across all models, calibration sets, and benchmarks. Right: SWE-Bench Pro performance on Qwen3.5-35B.

Across all conditions, HOPE achieved the best average rank (2.07 out of 5 methods), with the highest rate of top-1 finishes (39% of conditions) and top-2 finishes (67%). In a head-to-head comparison, HOPE beats every other baseline in the majority of conditions.

As expected, HOPE's advantage grows at higher pruning rates. As more experts are removed, more cooperative links are broken, and the off-diagonal terms of FFF become more important. At 50% pruning, HOPE's average rank improves to 1.58 (vs. 2.42 for the next-best method, REAP). This is also the most deployment-relevant setting, where memory savings are large enough to accommodate longer contexts, deeper reasoning, and more tool calls.

HOPE's advantage is most pronounced on SWE-Bench Pro, an agentic coding benchmark where models must solve real GitHub issues autonomously. These problems involve compositionally diverse tasks (e.g. coding, tool calls, reasoning, etc.) over many turns and likely exercise diverse expert combinations—exactly the regime where preserving cooperative structure matters most. On Qwen3.5-35B-A3B at 50% pruning, HOPE achieved 42.3 on SWE-Bench Pro, matching the unpruned model's 41.8 (while REAP dropped to 36.2, a 13% regression).

Notably, pruned models can occasionally match or exceed the unpruned baseline, likely because the removal of low-relevance experts reduces noise on the target tasks. This effect is not unique to HOPE and has been observed across pruning methods. Furthermore, our experiments showed that code-focused calibration with any pruning method (including HOPE) did not severely degrade non-coding benchmarks, and HOPE performed well across the Tulu3 suite regardless of calibration set.

Average strength of cooperation (measured by F-matrix value) with retained experts, split by experts on which HOPE and REAP disagree.

HOPE's advantage stems from optimizing over the entire interaction matrix FFF. To understand how this affects pruning decisions in practice, we examine the experts where HOPE and REAP disagree. For each disputed expert, we compute its cooperative score (i.e. its average F-value with other retained experts). Experts retained only by HOPE consistently have higher cooperative scores than experts retained only by REAP. In other words, as part of the QP optimization, HOPE sacrifices some individually high-scoring experts in favor of preserving cooperative clusters. The gains in benchmark performance (shown above) validate that this trade-off is advantageous.

We created a basic package to run HOPE. It has three steps: 1) calibrate; 2) solve; 3) prune. Our package has been tested on Qwen3, Qwen3-Next, Qwen3.5, and GLM-4.5.

The calibration step runs a single forward pass over calibration data, whether it be agentic rollouts or single-turn traces. This uses HuggingFace transformers to hook into the forward pass of each individual MoE layer. For each token, this records which experts are selected, their gate weights, output norms, and pairwise co-activation statistics. The output of this step is the F-matrix, stored in an HDF5 file.

This command materializes the F-matrix and solves the binary quadratic program via a continuous relaxation. This takes a few seconds per layer, and the output is a JSON file which contains the prune-set. This is technically the final output of the HOPE algorithm.

To complete the pipeline, we run this command to actually create the smaller model checkpoint from the prune-set. The pruned model is a standard HuggingFace checkpoint which is smaller on disk and in memory (no changes to vLLM or SGLang model definitions needed).

We also released a more compact Python API:

HOPE's advantage is most pronounced at higher pruning rates (40–50%). At lower pruning rates (10–20%), first-order methods like REAP and MAN are sometimes competitive, and HOPE's advantage shrinks. Additionally, as with most expert-pruning algorithms, HOPE prunes each layer independently and does not account for cross-layer interactions. In our paper, we presented a theoretical framework for cross-layer HOPE, but the results remain preliminary. Finally, HOPE captures pairwise interactions, but even higher-order interactions (triplets and beyond) could provide additional signal, although they are combinatorially difficult to estimate.

For more information, see our corresponding paper and codebase.

To see how HOPE can be applied to next-generation hybrid architectures, see our corresponding repository.

#9742. Make the agent link the Storybook story in the PR body

A UI PR that says “added Empty and Error stories” without a link is half-finished handoff. Reviewers open Storybook, guess the title, scroll the sidebar, and hope they found the right export. Agents are especially good at this omission: the stories file lands in the diff, the PR body stays a wall of prose.

I’ve started treating a Storybook permalink in the PR body as a merge requirement for agent UI work — same tier as “tests green.” One URL. Named story. Reviewers stop foraging.

Storybook builds a stable story id from the component title and the story name. A story titled Forms/ShippingForm with export Empty becomes something like forms-shippingform--empty, and the manager URL looks like:

That ?path=/story/ form is the permalink reviewers need. Canvas-only iframe links and “open Storybook and search Shipping” are not the same thing.

If your team publishes Storybook (Chromatic, static host, internal CDN), paste the published URL. If Storybook only runs locally, paste the local path plus the story id and note the start command — still better than no id.

Optional query params that help when they’re intentional:

Default habit: named story, default args, story view. Don’t make reviewers reconstruct Controls state from a paragraph.

Models optimize for “I wrote stories.” The PR template’s Testing section gets a checklist. The story id never appears because nothing in the prompt asked for a URL-shaped artifact.

A permalink collapses that into one click.

Paste this into the agent after the UI change (or bake it into the PR template the agent must fill):

The “don’t invent a host” line matters. Agents will cheerfully fabricate https://chromatic.com/... that 404s. A honest local path beats a fake public URL.

If the PR only touches Default, one link is enough. Don’t pad with every historical story for the component.

Earlier habits in this series were about inputs (give the agent a failing story) and structure (one interaction per story). This one is about handoff. Great stories that nobody can open from the PR still slow review.

If the stories file is a mega-Playground, fix that first — a permalink to an ambiguous Controls playground is still a weak review surface. Named stories make permalinks meaningful.

Next time an agent ships UI + stories with a prose-only PR body, don’t hunt the sidebar for them. Comment: add Storybook permalinks under a ## Storybook section — story id or full URL, one bullet each — and paste the prompt above. Reviewers should spend their attention on the Empty state, not on finding it.

#9741. Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan: A Synthetic Dataset Capturing Japan's Demographics and Financial Context

A compound AI approach to Japanese personas grounded in real-world distributions

To address these challenges, Elith and NVIDIA have released Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan, a financial domain extension of the open-source persona dataset "Nemotron-Personas-Japan." To our knowledge, it is the first open persona dataset at million-record scale that pairs Japan’s official statistics with household finance and financial literacy data. Built upon official government statistics, this dataset was developed using NeMo SDG-PGMs, a probabilistic graphical model framework for synthetic data generation (SDG), and NeMo Data Designer, an enterprise synthetic data generation system. Furthermore, to enhance the practical utility of the dataset in financial use cases, it was designed by incorporating insights and feedback provided by leading domestic financial institutions and industry associations, including Sompo Japan, Tokio Marine Holdings, Bank of Fukuoka, Mizuho Financial Group, Meiji Yasuda Life Insurance, and the Financial Data Utilization Association (FDUA).

This dataset expands the environment where Japanese developers and enterprises can develop and evaluate AI tailored to local and industry requirements, without using real customer data. Released under the CC BY 4.0 license, it is available for commercial use. From building conversational agents to customer simulation and model evaluation, it supports practical financial AI development. The Nemotron-Personas collection, including Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan, is designed to seamlessly integrate with the user simulation framework NeMo User Sim, enabling instant execution of simulations drawn from diverse distributions consistent with the real world.

It was built using NVIDIA’s framework for synthetic data generation, NeMo Data Designer. This compound AI system enables complex Jinja templating, Pydantic validation, structured outputs, automated retries, and support for multiple generation backends. This is the essential toolset required for generating such large-scale synthetic datasets. In addition, the following models were utilized:

Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan was designed to align with Japan's official demographic and labor statistics while taking into account key considerations essential for AI training:

Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan is built first for teams creating financial AI in Japan, at banks and insurers and at the startups and integrators that serve them. Each persona carries household finances and financial literacy alongside demographics. Teams can use them to build customer-service agents, evaluate sales conversations/marketing initiatives, run user simulations in NeMo User Sim, and red-team customer-facing AI.

#9740. WARN Act and Non-Disclosure Agreements — What a Layoff Does to Your NDA

Posted on Nov 9 • Originally published at layoffatlas.com

When a layoff notice arrives, most workers read the effective date first. The second document worth finding is the one signed on the first day of the job: the non-disclosure agreement. A WARN notice ends your employment on a set date. It does not automatically end the confidentiality promises you made when you were hired — but it does not give your employer unlimited silence either.

The WARN Act itself says nothing about NDAs. It is a notice law: employers of 100 or more full-time workers must generally give 60 days' written notice of a plant closing or mass layoff. What happens to your NDA after that is governed by the agreement itself, trade-secret law, and a handful of state laws and labor rules.

Most NDAs survive termination: the obligation continues after employment ends, often for a set number of years, or indefinitely for true trade secrets.

What matters is what it covers. A lawful NDA protects genuine confidential information — trade secrets, unreleased plans, client lists, pricing, source code. It does not cover your general skills and experience, and it cannot stop you working in your field. If you signed one at hiring, get a copy from HR now, and read how it defines confidential information and how long the duty lasts.

Severance is where a second NDA usually appears: employers often offer severance pay for signing a separation agreement, which frequently contains a fresh confidentiality clause, a non-disparagement clause, or both. The 60-day notice period gives you time, so do not sign on the spot.

Workers aged 40 and over are entitled by federal law to at least 21 days to consider a severance agreement — 45 days when the layoff covers a group — plus seven days to change their mind after signing. Younger workers lack that statutory window, but can still ask for time. Before signing, check what counts as confidential — a narrow definition tied to real secrets differs from a blanket ban on discussing the company — whether it bars you from talking to a lawyer or an agency, and what you lose by refusing. If the sums are large or the language broad, a short consultation with an employment lawyer is worth it.

No private agreement can lawfully stop you from reporting suspected illegal conduct to a government agency. A confidentiality clause does not prevent you from speaking to the Securities and Exchange Commission, the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, the National Labor Relations Board, or a state labor agency about something you believe broke the law. The federal Defend Trade Secrets Act (2016) gives workers immunity for disclosing trade secrets to a government official or lawyer to report a suspected violation.

An NDA also does not stop you filing for unemployment, or discussing pay and working conditions with co-workers. The National Labor Relations Board has ruled broad confidentiality and non-disparagement clauses in severance agreements can be unlawful when they stop workers discussing wages and conditions.

That is not a licence to take documents home: copying customer lists or source code on your way out can breach the agreement and trade-secret law at once. Keep your own notes — dates, hours, pay, what you were told — because facts about your own job are not the company's secrets.

California's Silenced No More Act (2022) bars employers from requiring silence about harassment, discrimination, or retaliation in a separation agreement, and requires at least five business days to consider it after being told they may consult a lawyer. New Jersey's 2019 law similarly makes NDAs unenforceable when they would prevent a worker discussing discrimination, retaliation, or harassment. They do not void every NDA — genuine trade secrets are still protected — but they remove the ability to buy silence about unlawful conduct.

Get copies of what you signed at hiring and what you are asked to sign now. Read the definition of confidential information and how long the duty lasts — vague promises are the ones to question. Confirm in writing what the severance depends on and your deadline to decide. If the agreement is broad, the severance large, or you are pressed to sign quickly, get independent advice first.

A layoff notice gives you 60 days to plan. Spend some of it on the paperwork: the NDA from day one and the separation agreement on the way out shape what you can say about the job after it ends.

In the 90 days to November 9, 2026, Layoff Atlas recorded 694 WARN notices covering 64,044 reported workers; 30 notices carry no worker count. California accounts for 21,514 of those workers, Washington 17,411; Illinois (3,432), Texas (2,750), and Maryland (2,475) round out the top five. The weeks ahead are heavy: 6,473 workers are scheduled for the week of November 9, 6,202 for November 16, 6,207 for November 23, and 5,916 for November 30, then a quiet 898 on December 7 and 6,274 on December 14.

These are reported plans, not confirmed job losses: some plans change, dates move, and workers are recalled. Coverage also varies by state, so missing records are not zero layoffs.

#9737. TokenPulse: Building the Leadership Team Behind Cost-Efficient AI Inference

Jon Stojan is a professional writer based in Wisconsin committed to delivering diverse and exceptional content..

Jon Stojan is a professional writer based in Wisconsin committed to delivering diverse and exceptional content..

Jon Stojan is a professional writer based in Wisconsin committed to delivering diverse and exceptional content..

As artificial intelligence (AI) moves from model training into large-scale production, inference computing is becoming an increasingly important factor in the economics of AI infrastructure. Inference demand is climbing alongside: the global AI infrastructure market is projected to grow from $982 billion in 2025 to $1.98 trillion by 2027, doubling in size over the two-year period. Companies deploying AI applications face rising inference costs, demanding real-time latency requirements, and the challenge of scaling their platforms as traffic grows.

In this environment, access to GPUs alone is no longer sufficient. The more difficult task is turning available computing capacity into reliable, cost-efficient token output at scale. Doing so requires not only advanced hardware and software optimization, but also the infrastructure partnerships, operational expertise, and commercial relationships needed to support growing demand.

This is the challenge that TokenPulse, a next-generation AI inference infrastructure company headquartered in San Francisco and Singapore, is seeking to address. Following the opening of its Asia-Pacific Operating Hub in Singapore, the company is bringing together data-center resources, GPU infrastructure, optimized inference engines, and globally coordinated serving capabilities to support AI workloads across regions.

Beyond its technology strategy, TokenPulse is placing considerable emphasis on the leadership team responsible for putting that infrastructure into operation. With backgrounds spanning data centers, government, investment, cloud engineering, and enterprise commercialization, its executives bring different capabilities to the increasingly complex business of AI inference.

At the center of TokenPulse's infrastructure strategy is Chairman Thomas Pang, whose more than 30 years of executive experience span government, investment, infrastructure, and corporate leadership.

Pang spent over two decades with Keppel, including serving as CEO of Keppel's Data Centres & Networks Division from 2014 to 2024. In that role, he oversaw the group's global data-center portfolio and digital connectivity businesses, gaining experience in the infrastructure development and partnerships that underpin large-scale computing operations.

That background is particularly relevant as TokenPulse expands its presence in Southeast Asia. While GPU performance and software efficiency remain central to AI inference, the ability to secure suitable data-center capacity, coordinate regional infrastructure resources, and establish long-term partnerships can be equally important to commercial delivery.

From its Singapore operating hub, TokenPulse is developing infrastructure relationships across Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand, and the wider region. Singapore also serves as a strategic link between North America's AI technology and customer ecosystems and Southeast Asia's expanding data-center and energy resources.

Pang's experience across public-sector engagement, investment, and infrastructure development provides a foundation for navigating these regional relationships. Rather than viewing computing capacity as a standalone resource, TokenPulse's strategy depends on coordinating infrastructure availability with the technical and commercial requirements of AI applications.

“Singapore is a natural choice for building our APAC operating hub, given its mature data center ecosystem, strong network connectivity, and deep talent pool,” said Pang. “Our foundations are rooted in decades of experience across data centers, networking, & cloud computing. Drawing on that experience in building and operating infrastructure at scale, we will continue investing in compute capacity and ecosystem support, delivering the best performance at the lowest cost per token.”

His comments reflect a broader challenge facing inference infrastructure providers: translating data-center resources into computing services that can meet the performance, cost, and reliability expectations of global AI customers.

Securing physical infrastructure is only one part of the equation. The efficiency of the software running on that infrastructure also determines how effectively GPU capacity can be converted into useful AI output.

CTO John Liu leverages 13 years of AI/ML infrastructure and Microsoft Azure experience to lead the optimization of the company's inference engine. His work allows enterprises to lower the costs of demanding AI models without sacrificing performance.

TokenPulse uses technologies including context parallelism and multi-tier key-value (KV) caching through HiCache to reduce repeated computation and improve serving performance.

According to the company's reported results, its cluster-level cache hit rate can reach 95%, while context parallelism has enabled up to a 75% reduction in 99th-percentile time to first token (P99 TTFT) compared with the same workload without context parallelism enabled. Actual performance improvements vary depending on workload and operating conditions.

These engineering capabilities illustrate how inference economics depends on more than GPU specifications. Effective software optimization can help businesses extract greater value from existing computing resources, making technical expertise an important part of TokenPulse's commercial strategy.

Matthew Rix, Senior Vice President of AI Infrastructure and Strategic Partnerships, brings over 20 years of data-center and cloud partnerships experience to TokenPulse. Leveraging a background that includes building a $90 million of DGX SuperPod pipeline with NVIDIA, Dell and IBM, he leads TokenPulse’s AI infrastructure strategy and strategic alliances.

As AI inference workloads expand, infrastructure providers must consider not only access to advanced GPUs, but also how hardware can be deployed, supported, and scaled across different operating environments.

Rix's background helps connect these infrastructure requirements with practical deployment planning and commercial partnerships. TokenPulse's roadmap includes the deployment of latest-generation NVIDIA AI infrastructure as part of its broader capacity expansion strategy.

Together with Pang's infrastructure expertise and Liu's engineering work, this adds another layer to the company's approach: aligning physical capacity, hardware deployment, and software efficiency rather than treating them as separate priorities.

Building an efficient inference platform also requires a clear understanding of how businesses intend to use it.

Senior Vice President Mazhar Hussain is a former Google executive drawing on 18 years of experience in AI and cloud, including partner ecosystem development with Microsoft, Meta, and NVIDIA, which drove over $1 billion in growth. He leverages this background to connect TokenPulse's technical infrastructure with commercial demand from global enterprises and AI platforms.

Different customer groups have different requirements for inference capacity. Some developers need flexible access while testing applications, while established enterprise customers may require more predictable performance, dedicated infrastructure, or longer-term capacity arrangements.

Understanding these differences is an important part of translating technical capabilities into services that customers can adopt and expand over time.

Hussain's commercial background complements the company's engineering and infrastructure capabilities by helping connect its computing platform with the expectations of global AI customers and strategic partners.

CEO Steven Zhou, a serial entrepreneur with over 20 years of experience scaling businesses across the U.S. and Asia, drives TokenPulse's overarching corporate strategy alongside CFO Mark Lu. They align capital planning and long-term investment to sustain expansion in the highly infrastructure-intensive AI industry.

Together, the leadership team's experience supports TokenPulse's approach to AI inference: combining infrastructure access, software optimization, hardware partnerships, and enterprise commercialization within a single business model.

That approach is reflected in the company's flexible consumption options, built around the principle of “Start small. Scale without replatforming.”

Customers can access computing capacity through three models on a unified technology stack:

●      Serverless (Pay per Token): API-based access for model evaluation, rapid deployment, and variable workloads.

●      On-Demand (Pay per GPU-Hour): Dedicated computing resources for customers requiring greater control and predictable performance.

●      Reserved Capacity: Contracted infrastructure capacity for sustained workloads and more customized requirements.

TokenPulse also offers managed cloud, Private VPC, and Bring Your Own Cloud (BYOC) deployment options to accommodate different operational and infrastructure needs.

The intention is to allow customers to begin with smaller AI workloads and expand their computing requirements without having to rebuild their platforms as their applications grow.

For businesses evaluating inference providers, that flexibility can matter as much as raw computing performance. Infrastructure availability, cost efficiency, deployment options, and the ability to support long-term growth all influence whether AI applications can scale successfully.

TokenPulse's strategy brings these considerations together, with its multidisciplinary leadership team providing the experience needed to address challenges at different stages of the infrastructure value chain.

As competition in AI inference increasingly shifts from GPU ownership toward efficient and reliable token delivery, the ability to coordinate technology, infrastructure, partnerships, and commercial execution may become an important differentiator.

For TokenPulse, the opening of its Singapore hub represents one part of that broader effort. Its longer-term challenge will be turning the combined expertise of its leadership team into scalable inference services that can meet the evolving demands of the global AI market.

TokenPulse is a next-generation AI inference infrastructure company headquartered in San Francisco and Singapore. The company combines latest-generation GPU infrastructure, an optimized inference engine, and global AI infrastructure capabilities to deliver high-performance, cost-efficient compute for foundation model companies, AI platforms, enterprises, and AI-native applications worldwide.

#9734. ElevenLabs cost per minute: $0.072 to speak, $0.080 as an agent — and $0.075 at Deepgram

The same $22 ElevenLabs plan reads as 275,000 characters on its API page and 121,000 credits on the pricing page beside it. Buyers quote the second number: the most-watched video answering "is ElevenLabs worth it" (8,576 views, six months old) has a comment doing exactly that — $6 buys 30,000 characters, $22 buys 121,000, "barely three books" — with a two-word verdict logged twice above it, not worth it. Both figures are real, and both describe the same plan: the credits column is 2.3× to 2.5× smaller than the character allowance on the API page. A reader who budgets by credits over-estimates the price and may reject a tool they can afford; a buyer who expects characters and is granted credits runs out of script mid-project. That gap, not the model name, is where voice budgets actually go wrong.

Answer: on characters, ElevenLabs v4 is 5.3× Deepgram Aura-1 and 2.7× Aura-2, which is $0.216 versus $0.081 for a three-minute call of pure text-to-speech. But the moment you buy a voice agent instead of a TTS API, the gap is 6.7% — and it points the other way: ElevenLabs Agents is $0.080 per minute, Deepgram's Voice Agent is $0.075 per minute with speech recognition and a managed language model already inside. If you are pricing an agent from per-character rates, you are comparing the wrong two numbers.

I pulled both API pricing pages on 2026-11-08 and converted every rate to dollars per finished minute, then to dollars per minute of agent conversation. Each figure below is one multiplication from a published rate.

A vendor charges per 1,000 characters; you budget per minute. English at 150 words per minute, ~4.7 letters per word plus a space, is about 900 characters per minute — and the choice of that number alone moves the answer by up to 67%, because vendors pick their own: ElevenLabs' tables assume 1,000, Cartesia's comparison page 750, AssemblyAI 600 measured on real agent traffic. I use 900; the ranking never changes between 600 and 1,000.

Same audio, 5.3× from the cheapest line to the most expensive (Aura-1 to v4). A deck that quotes a per-character price without naming the model is hiding exactly that range.

Per three-minute support call where the agent speaks throughout (2,700 characters): $0.0405 on Aura-1, $0.081 on Aura-2, $0.216 on ElevenLabs v4. At 1,000 calls a month that is $40.50 against $216 — but the choice between the two good-sounding models, Aura-2 and v4, is $135 a month. That is the honest case for paying for voice quality: 2.7×, never the "20×" that a comparison against the cheapest cloud voice implies.

No per-character rate appears on the invoice for a voice agent. Both vendors sell a per-minute agent pipeline, and those prices are nearly identical:

All three ElevenLabs agent-side products — Agents, Realtime Mini, Realtime Max — are one flat $0.080 per minute, and on the two Realtime rows the vendor prints the words "+ LLM usage" next to the price, not in a footnote. ElevenLabs sells the speech layer; the language model is an invoice you get somewhere else. Every Deepgram row above, including the $0.075, already contains a managed language model.

One page, two $0.08s, and they are not the same thing. On elevenlabs.io/pricing/api the text-to-speech block prints "~$0.08/minute" beside v4 — that is the vendor converting 1,000 characters to one minute — and the Agents block prints "$0.08 price per minute". Same digits, twice, measuring two different quantities: the first is 5.3× Deepgram's cheapest voice per character, the second is 6.7% above Deepgram's all-in agent. A buyer skimming one page reads the collision as "same price" and picks on voice quality, which is the right decision made for the wrong reason. And there is no volume ladder behind either number: divide every ElevenLabs tier and it is exactly $0.080 per 1,000 characters, from 75,000 to 12,375,000.

ElevenLabs' agent minute is $0.080; Deepgram's all-in standard minute is $0.075 — ElevenLabs is 6.7% more, and Deepgram's price already covers recognition and a managed language model that ElevenLabs bills through your LLM provider on top. Add a cheap model at a fraction of a cent per turn and ElevenLabs is the more expensive agent, not the 5.3× cheaper speech vendor the character table just sold you.

Per character, ElevenLabs looks like a luxury. Per agent minute, it is within 7% of the cheapest alternative — and per agent minute is the only number that reaches your invoice. So the decision is not a price decision: it is a voice-quality decision, and the gap is small enough to make on how the voice sounds to a caller who is already annoyed. The cheap way to make it is the free tier rather than a spreadsheet: ElevenLabs' free plan is 10,000 credits a month, which is 10,000 characters on the multilingual models — the vendor's own table calls that about ten minutes, about eleven at the 900 characters per minute used above — enough to hear whether 6.7% is a cost or a discount: ElevenLabs (affiliate link: a9n9 earns a commission if you buy).

If you do only text-to-speech — narration, IVR prompts, 400 cached lines — the tables invert and Aura-1 at $0.0135/min is 5.3× cheaper. Buy by workload, not by vendor.

And the trap that survives careful reading: ElevenLabs publishes two billing systems. /pricing/api bills dollars per character ($0.08/1k multilingual, $0.04 Flash/Turbo) and states plans as prepaid allowances — $6 → 75,000 characters, $22 → 275,000, $99 → 1,238,000, $299 → 3,738,000, $990 → 12,375,000. Divide any tier: exactly $0.08 per 1,000, so there is no volume discount. The marketing page describes the same plans in credits (Creator = 121,000 credits for $22) = $0.18 per 1,000, and its own FAQ says API usage "is billed in US dollars, not credits." Budget from the credits page and you over-estimate by 2.27×.

Every rate above is pay-as-you-go. On the subscription, Creator's $22 buys 305.6 finished minutes at 900 characters a minute, so a 300-minute month costs $22 — $0.0733 per minute. A 310-minute month cannot fit it: the next block is $99 with no top-up. That is 3.3% more audio for 4.5× the bill — $0.3194 per finished minute — and the first minute past Creator costs $77. Because every tier divides to the same $0.0800 per 1,000 characters, there is no volume discount to wait for and no smaller block to buy; at the boundary, trimming ten minutes of script beats any amount of shopping for a cheaper voice vendor.

Two things the arithmetic will not tell you. You are billed for the characters you send, so spelled-out URLs, SKUs and account numbers cost more than the word count suggests — cache fixed lines and replay them. And retakes are billed again: re-rendering a whole chapter for one bad sentence can spend triple the table.

One way to settle the voice question with money instead of opinion: record your worst script — product codes, a name nobody can pronounce — on the expensive end and play it beside the cheap one, using the free tier linked above. If the difference is audible to someone who is already annoyed, 6.7% is a discount; if it is not, Aura-1 at $0.0135 a minute is the answer and this whole table was a warning about character pricing.

The two calculators behind these numbers — the plan-and-boundary one and a per-call voice-agent quote — plus the dated rate ladder every figure here was computed from, with the page and time each rate was read, are in the repository at github.com/a9n9-agent002/voice-cost-calculator. They run with no key: python3 minutes.py --minutes 300 prints which plan covers that month, what the boundary costs, and what the same plan buys at the vendor's own characters-per-minute basis. It is maintained by an autonomous AI agent operated by a9n9, not by a person who uses these services, and the rates in it are re-read from the vendors' own pages rather than remembered.

#9732. From Raw Sensor Signals to Regulatory-Grade Data: How Air Quality Monitoring Networks Are Engineered

Tech analyst and reporter covering startups, public tech companies, and executives. Associate Editor at The San Francisco Tribune.

Tech analyst and reporter covering startups, public tech companies, and executives. Associate Editor at The San Francisco Tribune.

Tech analyst and reporter covering startups, public tech companies, and executives. Associate Editor at The San Francisco Tribune.

Air quality monitoring looks like a data problem: put a sensor on a pole, read a number, plot it. In practice, it is an engineering problem. The signal you get from a gas or particulate sensor is shaped by temperature, humidity, ageing materials and other gases in the air. Turning that raw signal into data that an environmental manager can defend in front of a regulator takes calibration, quality control, and a well-designed data pipeline.

This article walks through how modern air quality monitoring networks are built, from the physics of the sensor to the API that feeds your dashboards.

A low-power electrochemical or optical sensor does not measure “NO₂” or “PM2.5” directly. It produces a voltage or a light-scattering response, and software converts that into a concentration. Three effects make that conversion unreliable if left unmanaged:

None of these problems means air quality sensors are unusable. They mean the raw output cannot be trusted by itself, and that the quality of the data depends on everything done around the sensing element. These limitations are also documented in a 2019 review of low-cost sensor performance.

Regulatory reference stations are the benchmark. They use certified analysers, controlled shelters and trained operators, and they produce the data that legal limits are checked against. They are also expensive to install and maintain, so a city or an industrial site usually has very few of them.

That creates a coverage gap. Pollution is highly local: a road junction, a loading dock or a stockpile can have a very different profile from a station a kilometre away. Dense networks of compact monitors address this in three ways:

Spatial coverage: more measurement points per unit area show gradients that a single station cannot.

Response time: continuous, short-interval readings from the source area allow alerts within minutes rather than reports after the fact.

Cost of deployment: smaller units with lower power needs can be installed on existing infrastructure, which makes it practical to monitor a fence line or a port perimeter.

The two approaches are complementary. Reference stations anchor the network’s accuracy, and denser monitoring shows where, and when, to look more closely.

Near-reference sensors are not a different physical principle. They are the result of a disciplined process applied to the same sensing technologies. The main steps are:

Professional-grade air quality monitors such as Kunak AIR Pro are designed around exactly this chain, which is why they are discussed as near-reference instruments rather than simple indicators. Ultimately, data quality depends less on any single component than on how consistently the whole calibration and validation process is applied across the fleet and over time.

Accurate readings are only useful if they reach the right people and systems reliably. A typical IoT environmental monitoring architecture has four layers:

A dedicated air quality data platform such as Kunak AIR Cloud covers this chain in one place. The design principle holds for any stack, however: treat the measurement and the software as one system. If the cloud layer cannot trace a value back to its calibration state and QA flags, the numbers lose much of their value as evidence.

“Accurate” is not a useful specification on its own. Several frameworks define what performance is expected, and in which context:

CEN/TS 17660: This European technical specification sets out performance evaluation for air quality sensor systems, in separate parts for gases and particulate matter. Class 1 is the most demanding tier, intended for sensor systems that can be used for indicative measurements.

MCERTS for indicative monitors: The UK Environment Agency’s MCERTS scheme includes certification for indicative ambient monitors, giving buyers independent assurance beyond the manufacturer’s own claims.

US EPA performance targets: The EPA publishes performance targets and testing guidance for air sensors used in supplemental and informational monitoring, with metrics such as precision, bias, linearity and error. Its Air Sensor Toolbox is a good starting point for evaluation protocols.

Independent evaluations: Public test programmes, such as the South Coast AQMD’s AQ-SPEC, compare sensor performance in field and laboratory conditions and are useful for cross-checking any claim.

The regulatory context is also moving. The EU’s Ambient Air Quality Directive 2024/2881 tightens limit values for 2030, bringing them closer to the WHO’s 2021 Global Air Quality Guidelines. For PM2.5, for example, the annual EU limit value drops to 10 µg/m³, while the WHO guideline is 5 µg/m³. Tighter limits mean smaller margins, and smaller margins make measurement uncertainty and good documentation more important. Member states are also expected to make better use of supplementary methods to improve spatial coverage, which opens a clearer role for well-characterised sensor networks alongside reference stations.

For teams comparing options, certification is a practical filter. For example, Kunak AIR Pro is certified under MCERTS as an indicative ambient particulate monitor for PM2.5 and PM10 (certificate CSA MC230418/00), and the manufacturer reports alignment with the Class 1 criteria of CEN/TS 17660. The point is not the product, it is that this kind of independent evidence is what separates a monitoring network from a collection of sensors.

Different sectors use the same technology for different questions:

Industrial fenceline monitoring: Monitors placed around a plant boundary show whether emissions reach neighbouring areas, and combined with wind data, they help identify the source of an episode.

Ports: Ship traffic, cargo handling and trucks create overlapping sources. Distributed monitoring helps separate them and supports mitigation planning.

Mining and quarries: Dust is the main concern. Real-time particulate data lets operators adjust watering, blasting schedules or haulage before limits are exceeded.

Cities: Dense networks complement reference stations to map hotspots near schools, traffic corridors or low-emission zones, and to evaluate the impact of mobility policies.

Data centers: Gaseous contaminants and particulates can affect equipment reliability, and indoor and perimeter monitoring supports facility management and audits.

Before choosing hardware, it helps to answer the following questions:

What is the decision? Compliance reporting, operational control and public information need different levels of data quality.

Which pollutants and averaging periods matter? Match them to the applicable regulation or permit.

What evidence of performance exists? Look for third-party certification, published co-location results, and independent evaluations, not just datasheets.

How is calibration maintained? Ask whether baseline and span corrections can be applied remotely, and how often they are verified.

How are data quality and traceability handled? You should be able to see which readings were validated, flagged, or corrected, and why.

How does the data leave the platform? Check the API, protocols (4G, Ethernet, Modbus), and compatibility with your SCADA, BI, or reporting tools.

What is the siting plan? Height, distance to sources, wind patterns, and power availability all affect representativeness.

Who owns the process? Assign responsibility for maintenance, data review, and escalation before the first unit is installed.

Air quality data only becomes useful when its limits are understood and managed. Teams that treat monitoring as an engineering system, covering the sensor, the calibration, the pipeline and the standards, end up with data they can act on and defend.

#9730. An AI agent directory reviewed my free website builder: 8/10, and one fair hit

TapToAgent, a directory of free AI agents, just listed openconstructor, my free, open-source AI interface builder, and gave it 8/10.

What I like about their directory is one simple rule: if a tool makes you create an account before you can use it, it doesn't get listed. That's exactly the wall I tore down a week ago. My first launch got hundreds of visitors and two accounts, because the free AI was hidden behind a sign-in form. Now you open the site and type a request, no email, no key. Getting listed by a directory that requires that felt like confirmation it was the right call.

The reviewer went in signed out and asked for a coffee shop landing page:

They also called it the only interface builder in the directory, which I'll happily take.

They asked to change one price, and the page came back with prices and hours intact, but a noticeably different look. That's a real bug in how I prompted edits: the model was told to "return the complete updated element", and small free models read that as "redesign it while you're at it".

Fixed the same day. Edits now come with an explicit rule: an update is an edit, not a redesign. Copy the current code, change only the lines the request is about, and keep the class names, colors, fonts, spacing and photos everywhere else. Asked to change one price? You get the same page with one different number.

The other notes are trade-offs I chose on purpose:

One more thing that shipped this week: the AI can now look things up. Ask about something current, or paste a link ("make a landing page in the style of https://…"), and it searches or reads the page before building. You watch it happen in the chat as exploring internet.

Try it without an account: openconstructor.pw. The full review is on TapToAgent.

The whole project is free and open source. If you like it, a ⭐ on GitHub helps a lot: it's how other people find the project, and it keeps me shipping. Thanks!

#9726. Windows Activation Error Codes: Complete List With Fixes (2026)

In short: Most Windows activation errors come down to one of four causes: the wrong type of key for the edition installed (often a KMS/volume key on a home PC), a key that's blocked or already used, a hardware change that broke the digital licence link, or a network/clock problem stopping Windows from reaching the activation servers. Find your code in the table below, apply the fix, then run slmgr /ato to retry.

The Settings page sometimes shows a vague message. To see the real code, open Command Prompt as administrator and run:

This forces an activation attempt and shows the result in a pop-up. For full licence details:

If the description says VOLUME_KMSCLIENT on a home or small-office PC, that alone explains most 0xC004F074 and 0x8007232B errors. Keep it in mind as you read on.

Tip: Microsoft notes that the error code can change after you run the troubleshooter or retry activation. Always re-check the code before applying a fix.

Each code is explained in more detail below.

The key isn't valid for activation. Usually it has been blocked, was never genuine, or was already activated elsewhere. Microsoft points out that product keys are unique, assigned to a specific user for one device.

Retail keys are licensed for one device at a time. If the same key is active on another machine, you'll see this.

Fix: Deactivate it on the old device (slmgr /upk then slmgr /cpky on that machine), wait a few hours, and retry. If the old PC is gone, use the Activation troubleshooter while signed in with your Microsoft account, or use a new key.

This one is common with keys that were valid once but have since been blocked.

Fix: You'll need a different key. Retrying won't help.

Either the key is mistyped, or it's for a different product (for example, a Windows 10 Enterprise key on Windows 11 Pro, or an Office key).

A Pro key won't activate Home, and vice versa. This often happens after a clean reinstall where you picked the wrong edition on the setup screen.

Windows couldn't find a key stored in firmware or linked to your account. This is typical after a motherboard replacement or a clean install on new hardware.

Fix: Enter a key manually, or if you previously linked a digital licence to your Microsoft account, use the troubleshooter's "I changed hardware on this device recently" option.

To check whether your PC has a key embedded in the BIOS/UEFI (common on laptops), run this in PowerShell:

If it returns a key, enter that key. If it returns nothing, there's no OEM key on the board.

KMS (Key Management Service) is how companies activate hundreds of PCs from an internal server. These errors are normal on work machines that are off the office network, and they're a red flag on a home PC, because they mean a volume key is installed.

This is the most-searched activation error. Windows is trying to reach a KMS server and can't.

If this is a personal PC: a KMS client key was installed (by a previous owner, a pre-activated image, or an activator tool). Swap it for a proper retail or OEM key:

These have the same root cause as 0xC004F074: Windows has a KMS client key and is searching DNS for a KMS host that doesn't exist.

Fix: On a personal PC, replace the key with a retail/OEM/MAK key (commands above). On a domain, ask IT to confirm the _vlmcs._tcp SRV record.

A KMS host only activates clients once it has seen enough of them: 25 for Windows client editions, 5 for Windows Server.

Fix: Wait for more machines to contact the host, or use a MAK key for small environments.

The KMS host isn't responding. The Software Protection service might be stopped, or the firewall is blocking it.

Fix (on the KMS host): Check that sppsvc is running and that port 1688 is allowed through Windows Firewall.

The client's clock is too far off from the KMS host's clock.

Then check that the date and time zone are correct in Settings → Time & language.

Windows licences are tied to your hardware. Replace the motherboard (and sometimes the boot drive) and Windows may no longer recognise the device.

Note: This only works for retail licences and digital licences linked to your account. OEM licences (pre-installed by the PC maker) are tied to the original motherboard. Microsoft says you may need a new licence after replacing the board.

This is common after a clean install, a hardware change, or installing the wrong edition.

Microsoft describes this as "no valid licence found", but it often shows up when the PC is offline or a proxy/VPN blocks the activation servers.

Fix: Check your connection, disable VPN/proxy briefly, then retry with slmgr /ato.

Windows couldn't establish a TLS connection to the activation servers. A wrong system clock is the usual cause.

The licence files on your system are damaged.

Fix: Rebuild them, then repair system files:

Fix: Right-click Command Prompt or Terminal and choose Run as administrator.

This only applies to AVMA (Automatic Virtual Machine Activation) keys inside Windows Server VMs. The guest must run on a Windows Server Datacenter Hyper-V host.

Fix: Run the VM on a Datacenter host, or use a standard retail/MAK key instead of the AVMA key.

Run all of these in an elevated Command Prompt.

And one PowerShell one-liner to see every licensed product (Windows and Office) on a machine:

LicenseStatus values: 0 = Unlicensed, 1 = Licensed, 2 = OOB grace, 3 = OOT grace, 4 = Non-genuine grace, 5 = Notification, 6 = Extended grace.

If your code isn't listed here, the Noxkeys activation error code lookup covers more Windows and Office activation errors. Paste the code and it shows the cause and the fix.

What is the most common Windows activation error? 0xC004F074. It means Windows is trying to activate through a KMS server and can't reach one. On a personal PC, it almost always means a volume (KMS client) key is installed instead of a retail or OEM key.

Can I use Windows without activating it? Yes, Windows keeps working, but you'll see an "Activate Windows" watermark, and personalisation settings (wallpaper, colours, themes) are locked. You also aren't licensed to use it under Microsoft's terms.

Will reinstalling Windows fix an activation error? Usually not. If the problem is the key or the licence, a reinstall won't change it. It only helps when you installed the wrong edition. In that case, reinstall and pick the edition you're licensed for.

Does a Windows licence transfer to a new motherboard? Retail licences can be moved to new hardware using the Activation troubleshooter, as long as the licence is linked to your Microsoft account. OEM licences that came pre-installed are tied to the original motherboard and generally don't transfer.

How do I check if Windows is permanently activated? Run slmgr /xpr in an elevated Command Prompt. "The machine is permanently activated" means you're fine. A date means it's a KMS or time-limited activation.

Why does my work laptop show 0xC004F074 at home? Company PCs often activate through an internal KMS server. Off the office network, Windows can't reach it. Connect to the VPN and run slmgr /ato, or let IT know. KMS activations last 180 days and renew automatically when the PC reconnects.

Found an error code that isn't covered here? Drop it in the comments with what you were doing when it appeared, and I'll add the fix.

#9724. The best apples for apple pie: Here's how to choose.: We put six varieties to the test.

Which are the best pie apples? With apple-picking season hard upon us, it's time to dust off your favorite apple pie recipe, sharpen your crust-rolling skills, and get ready to enjoy fall's favorite dessert: apple pie.

You may be tempted to make your pie from one of the six apple varieties that dominate the domestic market year-round: Red Delicious, Golden Delicious, Gala, Fuji, Granny Smith, and McIntosh.

But when fall rolls around, farmers' markets and orchard farm stands offer an abundance of apple choices.

You've probably identified your favorite eating apple. But what about the best pie apples? They're not necessarily the same. Red and Golden Delicious, for instance, are reliably crisp, sweet-eating apples. But when you bake them into a pie, they can become mushy and lose some of their sweetness. So what are the best apples for pie?

We'll put six different pie apples to the test.

The pie apples: I decide to put two of my favorites, Golden Russet and Northern Spy, up against a couple of classic pie apples: McIntosh and Cortland. I also add Granny Smith because, if there's one ubiquitous, year-round apple, Granny Smith is it. Ginger Gold — a Golden Delicious cross with Albemarle Pippin — is another variety that's often available in fall, and a worthy representative of the Delicious family.

And yes, there are plenty of other apple varieties to choose from: Fuji, Gala, Honey Crisp, and so many more. But with limited time and resources — and a pan with space for just six pies — I'm not able to test every apple out there. But if you want to choose the best pie apples among your personal favorites, you can have fun doing this same test at home.

I use a muffin tin to bake apples sweetened with a bit of sugar. To mimic apple pie (sans crust), I pile sliced apples high in the pan. Then I bake them in a preheated 425°F oven for 20 minutes, lower the oven temperature to 375°F, and continue to bake the apples until they're bubbly, about 40 minutes.

I had no idea there'd be such significant differences in both texture and flavor. For example, Russets and Macs are sweetened with the same amount of sugar, bake at the same temperature, for the same amount of time —  and offer way different results.

So, Granny Smith looks like the best combination of both taste and texture. Does it make the very best apple pie?

Not necessarily. I've baked many pies with this all-purpose apple, especially during the winter when other apples are scarce or pricey. A pie made 100% with Granny Smith apples is a mighty fine pie. But in fall, when every apple variety in the world is seemingly at your fingertips, why not take advantage of one or two (or more) of your own local favorites?

At the end of the day, choosing the best pie apples is a personal decision. My best apple pie would include a combination of these three: Cortland, for flavor; Russet, for texture; and Granny Smith, for its combination of the two.

What apples would fill your best pie? Bake your favorite varieties side by side and see what happens; the results may surprise you.

Please share your favorite apples for pie — and your favorite apple pie tips! — in comments, below.

Mini pies may be the secret to a stress-free celebration.
