    #9606. How to proof bread in the oven: Common challenge, simple solution.

    During proofing, bread and other yeasted doughs do best in a temperature-controlled, humid, draft-free environment. Your kitchen counter may not cut it (especially in colder months), but is there a corner of your kitchen that fits that description? Yes, your oven — and you don’t even need to fire it up!

    Yeast dough is happiest when rising at temperatures between 75°F and 78°F. It will certainly rise in cooler or warmer temperatures. But for most doughs, that range is optimum for both yeast development and bread flavor.

    Your oven’s interior will pretty much mirror room temperature. And depending on the time of year (or how much you use air conditioning), that temperature could be pretty cool—too cool for yeast’s comfort.

    To get the oven up to that ideal proofing temperature, people often turn to a couple of different methods. I decided to try a bunch of them to see which is best — and helpfully, there was a clear winner.

    It’s tempting to simply preheat the oven for a minute or so to warm its interior; but not only is this hit-and-miss (How long should I leave it on? Will the oven get too hot?), it’s ineffective; the heat quickly dissipates once you turn the oven off.

    Enter your oven light. When turned on, your oven light’s slow, gentle heat will gradually warm the oven to the desired temperature. After trying a number of different methods for proofing bread in the oven, including several listed below, this was my clear favorite because it created the ideal temperature (not too hot, not too cold), maintained that temperature for several hours, and was essentially failproof (no overshooting the temp, for example!).

    It can take your oven a while to reach the desired temperature, especially if your kitchen is cold to begin with. With so many variables — season, climate, kitchen, oven — you’ll want to do a simple experiment to determine your own best method for turning your oven into an effective, efficient proof box:

    Take your oven’s temperature before turning on the light. Then turn on the light and measure the temperature again at 15-minute intervals, to see just how quickly the light warms things up. For reference, the light in my electric oven takes about an hour to raise the oven’s interior temperature by 10 degrees, and another hour to raise it an additional five degrees; your results will probably vary a bit.

    Warm your oven to about 80°F before turning off the light. Over the next couple of hours, the temperature will gradually drift down by about 10 degrees, giving your rising dough plenty of time in and around that 75°F to 78°F sweet spot.

    Once you know how to warm your oven using only its lightbulb, think about maintaining humidity: Dry dough can develop a tough skin, which inhibits rising.

    If you’re proofing dough in a bowl (or later, a shaped loaf in a pan), cover it with a clear plastic shower cap or reusable plastic bowl cover. Whatever you use, make sure it's large enough to form a “poof” on top, so the cover doesn’t touch the rising dough.

    For shaped rolls (or anything else in a large, flat pan), use an extra-large shower cap; or simply drape the pan with well-greased plastic wrap, waxed paper, or parchment.

    What if your oven doesn’t have a light, the lightbulb only lights when you open the oven door, or it’s a “cool” LED bulb?

    Then your best bet is a pan of boiling water set on the lowest rack, which will both warm and humidify your oven’s interior. Place the bread dough on the oven’s middle rack; no need to cover it.  Set a shallow pan (e.g., 9" x 13" pan) on the lower rack, and add four cups of boiling water. Quickly close the oven door.

    Your oven’s temperature will immediately rise by about 30 degrees, which will probably be warmer than you want. Cool it down by opening the door wide for about five minutes; the temperature should drop about 15 degrees.

    As the water in the oven cools, the air around it cools, too. But it happens so gradually that your oven should still remain sufficiently warm for the one to two hours your bread typically needs to rise. For longer-rising breads, simply switch out the cool water with another pan of hot water, if necessary.

    Some ovens actually have a proof setting or proofing drawer. I don’t always love using this setting, though: Most are programmed to temperatures ranging from 90°F to 100°F, far warmer than yeast dough’s optimal 75°F to 78°F. For best results, figure out how long it takes to reach about 80°F, then turn it off.

    Tip #1: If you have to open the oven door to check your rising dough, don’t worry. Unlike the huge 15- to 20-degree drop you experience when opening a fully heated oven, the temperature inside your light- or steam-warmed oven will only drop by a degree or two.

    Tip #2: Typically, you don’t preheat your oven with rising dough inside. So when your dough is close to fully risen, remove it from the oven and set it somewhere safe. (If there’s room, the top of your fridge is both warm and out of harm’s way.) Timed just right, your bread will be perfectly proved by the time the oven finishes preheating.

    Tip #3: To prevent someone from killing your rising dough by turning on the oven (say, to warm their leftover pizza), write “NO!” on a sticky note and affix it to the oven’s start button. Really!

    For the highly passionate bread baker (or a small baking business), an electronic proof box like the Brod & Taylor Proofer Pro is a step up from proofing dough in the oven. It controls temperature with exquisite precision, from cold-proofing (down to 41°F) for those overnight ferments up to 122°F for an express warmup, all while ensuring perfect humidity. Wi-Fi and programmable timers let you control your dough’s development for up to eight days. It’s literally set it and forget it — the process is simple, but the results are simply amazing.

    Still looking for a warm, draft-free spot for your rising bread dough? Think beyond your oven to other major appliances: Both your clothes dryer and dishwasher can double as a proof box!

    Cover photo by Mark Weinberg; food styling by Liz Neily.

    #9604. Sweet Potato Casserole

    Move aside, other casseroles—sweet potato casserole ranks at the very top of my list when it comes to Thanksgiving sides. I'll be coming back to this recipe time and time again, thanks to its buttery pecan topping. It’s still plenty sweet (thanks to the brown sugar), but not enough to make the sweet potatoes taste like straight-up dessert.

    What People Are Saying:“I made this for a Thanksgiving carry in a couple of years ago which was a hit, and just put it in the oven for this years dinner that I’m hosting! Delicioso, my family love this version the best. Thank you!☺️” - dmartin0958214

    After preheating the oven and greasing a baking dish with cooking spray, place your sweet potatoes in a large pot and cover with water. Bring them to a boil, then reduce the heat to medium-low and simmer until the potatoes are tender and you can poke them with a fork. Drain the water, then let them cool slightly before transferring to a large bowl. Add the butter to the potatoes, then mash with a potato masher or 2 forks.

    Mash until you reach your desired consistency (I prefer it smooth with a few chunks). Once they’ve reached the consistency you’re looking for, add eggs, milk, brown sugar, salt, nutmeg, and vanilla and stir until smooth. Once mixed, transfer to the prepared baking dish.

    In a medium bowl, mix all of the topping ingredients together until combined.

    Once combined, sprinkle the topping over the sweet potato mixture. Bake the casserole until it is warmed through and the topping is golden brown, then serve immediately while warm.

    The full list of ingredients & instructions can be found in the recipe below.

    This is a great make-ahead Thanksgiving recipe to save yourself time (and energy) on the big day. Prep the casserole up to step 2, then refrigerate until you're ready to bake (we recommend no more than a few days ahead of time). When you're ready to bake, you can prepare and top with the crumbly topping.

    If you have any leftovers (which I can't imagine you would), put them in an airtight container—or cover your casserole dish—and refrigerate for three to five days. This casserole also freezes wonderfully. Similar to prepping it ahead, simply prepare your casserole and bake it without topping it with the pecan topping. Allow it to cool before covering and freezing. When you're ready to serve, simply thaw it in the fridge overnight, top it with the crumbly topping, and bake.

    #9603. These 7 Burger Chains Use Frozen Ground Beef — Is Your Favorite On The List?

    Fast food chains have undergone an interesting transformation in recent years. They're under increasing pressure from customers and regulators alike to offer more nutritious, less-processed food, and much of the debate centers on whether they use fresh or frozen beef in their kitchens. Certain chains, like Chipotle, have even made their commitment to fresh ingredients a central part of their brand identity. But while fresh meat is certainly having a moment, frozen burger patties aren't going anywhere any time soon.

    Frozen beef patties play a foundational role in the fast food industry. To operate on the scale of giants like McDonald's, which sells millions of burgers a day, it goes without saying that you're going to need a serious amount of beef. That's where frozen has a serious edge. Fresh, raw beef has a relatively short shelf life, whereas frozen beef can be stored for months. That makes frozen patties a practical way to keep up with demand and avoid having large quantities of meat spoil before they can be used. They also offer consistency. Because patties can be made to precise specifications and frozen until needed, they're uniform in size and weight, helping ensure that every burger cooks at roughly the same rate and comes out looking like the last.

    One of the biggest assumptions surrounding fresh and frozen beef is that fresh automatically means better. But this isn't really fair. Freezing beef doesn't do anything to its nutritional profile, and patties are often frozen soon after production to preserve their freshness. Better yet, some chefs even swear by cooking burgers from frozen for a juicier texture and perfectly browned crust. Bet you didn't see that coming. If you still don't believe us, odds are that one of your favorite fast food burgers is living proof of this.

    As the largest fast food chain in the U.S., it probably won't come as much of a surprise that McDonald's relies heavily on frozen beef for its burgers, as well as breakfast items like its McMuffins, McGriddles, and bagels. Its frozen beef patties are cooked for around 40 seconds between two heated metal plates before being transferred to heated holding cabinets — that's right, McDonald's patties aren't made-to-order. For decades, this was standard practice across the menu, but in March 2018, the chain shook things up by officially rolling out fresh, never-frozen beef for its Quarter Pounder line.

    Burger King trails McDonald's as the second-largest burger chain in the U.S., but one area where it hasn't followed its rival's lead is fresh beef. While McDonald's offers one fresh option, Burger King still uses frozen beef across its entire burger menu. The patties are shaped and flash-frozen at centralized processing facilities before being shipped to individual restaurants. And despite the chain's famous claim that its burgers are "flame-grilled," that description doesn't tell the whole story. Rather than being grilled individually over an open flame, the frozen patties travel along a conveyor belt through a flame-broiling oven, where they're exposed to gas flames as they cook. It's this process that gives Burger King burgers their distinctive charred exterior and smoky flavor.

    Famous for early adoption of the fast-food drive-thru intercom system (which In-N-Out pioneered), Jack in the Box is best known for its delightfully eclectic menu, which hosts everything from tacos and curly fries to, of course, burgers. There are plenty of unique options to choose from, including the Sourdough Jack, served on toasted sourdough bread, and its newer line of trendy smash-style burgers. But one thing they all have in common is that their patties arrive at the kitchen frozen. So don't expect to find any fresh beef in Jack in the Box. The chain sticks to old-school griddling on a flat-top, but at the same time, it has piloted a batch of futuristic burger-flipping robots at certain locations in San Diego.

    A trip to Dairy Queen is never a bad idea when you're craving something sweet and frozen, but did you know that you can also order a burger to go with your Blizzard? Despite revealing that its burgers don't contain human meat (yes, this really happened), the chain is yet to share whether its beef patties arrive fresh or frozen. Given that we're talking about Dairy Queen here, you'd be forgiven for assuming they spend some time chilling in a freezer. And according to one self-identified employee, that's exactly the case. "[The patties] come frozen," they revealed in a Reddit comment. "We have a 'grill' where we put the patties on a conveyor belt that goes over a flame. Then, they drop down from the machine into baskets, where we put them in a warmer with other patties."

    White Castle holds an iconic place in American fast food history as one of the country's oldest burger chains. Founded in 1921, the chain originally used fresh beef, but it didn't take long to make the switch to more convenient frozen patties in 1931. Today, White Castle might not be on the same level as giants like McDonald's and Burger King, but we'll give it points for originality. Its cooking method is truly unlike anything you'll find at most other burger chains. First, a bed of onions is spread across a hot grill, followed by the frozen beef patties, with the buns placed on top. Rather than being seared directly against the cooking surface, the patties are steamed by the moisture rising from the onions. The small holes punched into each patty allow the steam to pass through, cooking the beef from below while warming the buns above.

    Everything about Sonic is gloriously retro, but there's nothing old-school about how the chain prepares its burgers. Before your burger is (literally) rolled out to your car, workers pull the patties straight from the freezer and place them on a flat-top grill, flipping them as they cook. Like many frozen fast-food patties, Sonic's burgers are also perforated with small holes. To those who have never worked in a fast-food kitchen before, these little bumps and ridges might look alarming at first, but there's really nothing to worry about. They're simply there to help the frozen patties cook more quickly and evenly.

    Carl's Jr. is a SoCal institution and has been serving up burgers since 1941. Like Burger King, the frozen patties are passed through a gas-flame conveyor belt, known as charbroiling. Though fans might be disappointed to learn that the chain's (rather pricey) burgers start out frozen, Carl Jr. is actively looking to level up its quality by promising that each and every burger will eventually be cooked-to-order. This means that customers will receive a hotter, fresher burger rather than a batch-cooked one that's been left sitting forgotten in a heating cabinet. As of writing, Carl's has released no official statement on whether the so-called "Burger Revolution" also includes non-frozen patties.

    #9601. The secret to make-ahead pie crust? Pie crumbs.: Get ahead on your pie baking right now.

    'Tis the season — to start thinking about holiday baking. And while this time of year is full of joy and celebration, it can also be stressful. We’re all searching for ways to get ahead of the curve, and one of the easiest? Make-ahead pie crust, made using pie crumbs.

    I first learned of this technique from a 90-something friend with whom I love to talk baking. Over lunch one day, something she said about pie captured my attention.

    "Did you ever hear of pie crumbs?" she asked. I admitted I hadn't — aside from the obvious: the scraps of pie crust left on the plate after the slice is gone. "My mother used to mix flour and salt and lard together to make this crumbly mixture that she'd store in a crock in the cellar. She called them her pie crumbs. When she wanted to make a pie, she'd just scoop out a few handfuls, add water, and roll out her crust."

    Sounds like a good make-ahead solution for 100 years ago — but now that we have easy access to freezers, why not just make pie dough and freeze it in ready-to-roll disks? A couple of reasons, actually.

    1) Pie crumbs allow you to make any amount of crust, from mini apple pies to a crust for a deep-dish 10" pie. With frozen disks, you're looking at a standard single crust — not always exactly what you want.

    2) Pie crumbs save time. Remove however much of the crumbly mixture you need (more on this below) from the freezer, and within 15 minutes the fat is soft enough that you can add water and roll out your crust. Compare that to the hours it takes to thaw and roll a frozen disk of prepared crust — not to mention the elbow grease if your crust isn’t fully thawed.

    3) Pie crumbs can be more stable in the freezer than pie crust disks. Why? Because without the added water, no ice crystals form. Ice crystals can damage the flour/water matrix, leading to changes in its structure (which can then potentially lead to changes in your pie crust).

    Oh, and one other reason I like pie crumbs: If my friend's mother used them, they were probably a 19th-century kitchen time-saver. And I love the feeling of preserving and carrying forward our American baking traditions — even something as simple as a shortcut for pie crust.

    Choose a standard pie crust recipe: Our Classic Double Pie Crust recipe is good choice, but anything that involves cutting fat into flour (lard, shortening, butter, etc.) will work.

    Mix flour, salt, and shortening and/or butter: Follow your recipe up until all of the fat is incorporated into the flour. You should be left with a bowl of dry, crumbly dough that barely holds together when squeezed. If using butter, you should be able to see visible chunks scattered throughout the dough.

    Weigh the pie crumbs: If you’re making a large batch of pie crumbs, it’s helpful to weigh and label the total gram amount so that you can easily remove the amount of pie crumbs for a single pie crust as needed. Our Classic Double Pie Crust makes 488 grams of pie crumbs; that means 244 grams per single pie crust. Label these amounts on your freezer storage bag.

    Bag, label, and freeze the crumbs: Seal pie crumbs in an airtight, freezer-safe bag and place in the freezer, preferably in the back where it won't be subject to warm air wafting over it each time you open the freezer door.

    Scoop crumbs out of the bag into a bowl: Whether one crust, two crusts, or one and a half, do the math and measure the crumbs based on your recorded gram amounts.

    Let the crumbs thaw for 15 to 20 minutes or so: Wait until the butter chunks feel barely pliable in your fingers.

    Add water and mix: Add water based on your original recipe amount, or just enough water to make a chunky mass when mixed. Squeeze and knead the dough briefly; all you're doing here is bringing the chunks together into one solid piece of dough.

    Roll the dough, place in a pan, and bake accordingly: From here, your pie crust is the same as any fresh-made crust and can be filled and baked or prebaked for a no-bake filling. (Bonus: Because the crumbs were frozen and remain cold as you work with them, there's no need to chill your rolled-out crust before filling and/or baking.)

    Fairly indefinitely, though the longer they're frozen, the more chance they have both to absorb freezer odors, and for the fats to start to go off. I've also found that, after about two weeks in the freezer, I need to add a touch more water than usual to bring the dough together — due to the drying effects inherent in freezing.

    With pie season hard upon us, now's the time to try pie crumbs for make-ahead pie crust. Or maybe you have another old-fashioned pie trick up your sleeve? Share your favorite tips in the comments, below.

    For detailed ingredient amounts for the crust demonstrated above, see our recipe for Classic Double Pie Crust.

    And if you're looking for additional time-saving ways to use your freezer in the run-up to the holidays, check out our recipe for Homemade Brown and Serve Rolls and Apple Pie with Make-Ahead Filling.

    #9599. Not Regular Butter: Popcorn Is Crispier When You Reach For This Ingredient

    We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

    Few snacks welcome modifications more readily than popcorn. You can go with a sweet cinnamon sugar recipe or a batch of spicy, chile-powder-covered kernels. Regardless of which direction you tweak the dish, fat is always welcome — it helps keep your seasoning on, but it's also simply delicious. Butter is the classic choice, but don't sleep on ghee, either. This foodstuff makes for an even crispier batch of the iconic movie theater snack.

    Also a dairy-based fat, ghee is clarified, which means the ingredient contains less water and more fat solids than butter. Ghee is further differentiated from clarified butter by way of the toasting process, which gives ghee a pleasant nutty flavor. Together, such qualities enhance popcorn in both taste and texture. Amplified crunch is the main draw. Once melted and applied to kernels, this translates to a much less soggy consistency. The popcorn still takes on a signature buttery flavor, but with less moisture clinging to each bite, the increased fat composition turns the snack extra crispy.

    Thankfully, working ghee into a batch of popcorn is straightforward. You can readily buy a jar of ghee on platforms like Amazon or Walmart, add around a tablespoon per a third cup of kernels, then pop away into a reimagined crunchy bite. It's a simple twist with a satisfying payoff.

    Ghee popcorn doesn't need much to shine; a simple sprinkle of salt rounds out a mouthwatering rendition of the snack. However, if you're a fan of a more complex popcorn rendition, don't shy away from bolder seasonings, too. Ghee is often used in South Asian cuisine, which means Indian spices are a natural start. The nutty notes make a terrific canvas for warm flavors like cinnamon, coriander, and cumin. Or for an even more dessert-like spin, mix in saffron, cardamom, and fennel — spices traditionally used to flavor nuts. Whipping up such blends is like making a spice-infused oil: You'll want to slowly bloom the components in the ghee.

    That said, don't rule out drawing from other cuisines with ghee, too. The milk-based fat can be the foundation of a smoky-sweet seasoning flavored with chile peppers and vanilla. Or you can incorporate a zesty complexity by using citrus rind instead. In addition to crisping up popcorn, ghee works as a remarkable flavor canvas, readily enveloping the snack in aromatics.

    #9598. Evaporated vs. condensed milk: What's the difference? : Navigating the canned dairy aisle.

    Navigating the dairy section at the grocery store is one thing, but when it comes to the canned stuff, how much do you know about the difference between evaporated milk and condensed milk?

    Before we discuss what sets evaporated milk apart from condensed milk, it’s important to discuss their similarities. Evaporated milk and condensed milk are both concentrated liquids made from fresh milk that gets heat-treated until about 60% of the water content is removed. The primary difference between the two is the amount of sugar they contain and their resulting texture.

    Evaporated milk will typically only contain lactose, or the naturally occurring sugars found in milk and dairy products. Condensed milk, on the other hand, contains around 40 to 45% added sugar. That contrast means condensed milk is much thicker (almost syrupy) and has a more pronounced sweet flavor (it’s no wonder it’s often referred to as sweetened condensed milk!), and evaporated milk runs watery in texture and is lighter in taste.

    Because of the extreme differences in the sugar content and consistency, evaporated milk and condensed milk cannot be used interchangeably. There will be a very noticeable difference if you use evaporated milk in a recipe that was written to use condensed milk, or vice versa.

    Using evaporated in a recipe that calls for condensed milk will result in a dessert that is too bland and watery, while using condensed milk in a recipe that calls for evaporated milk can make a dish way too sweet and thick. If your recipe calls for a very small amount (1 to 2 tablespoons) of condensed milk, you could get away with combining a spoonful of evaporated milk mixed with some sugar. But if your recipe needs one whole can of evaporated or condensed milk, be sure to use the correct type.

    If you want to learn more about – and celebrate – the differences between evaporated and condensed milk, make this Tres Leches Cake, which is a fantastic recipe that utilizes the two milks with heavy cream in a luscious cake soak for dessert. For a different dose of double the milk, you’ll want to try this creamy, custardy Vanilla Bean Flan.

    Evaporated milk provides richness and creaminess to dishes that are both sweet and savory. It’s often used to enrich custard-based pie fillings, like Hong Kong Egg Tarts, Delicata Squash Pie, and Pumpkin Pie. To round out your fall table and use up that can of evaporated milk, try the dairy ingredient in dinner recipes like Pumpkin Soup and Creamy Tomato Soup, or macaroni and cheese.

    If you have an unopened can of condensed milk, you can also make dulce de leche with it. One way to go about it is to let it simmer in a pan filled with water for a few hours: Learn how to make it here.

    #9596. Scrambled Eggs Are 10x Creamier & Fluffier With One Boxed Ingredient

    When you make scrambled eggs, heat, fat content, and your tools often require you to make them either fluffy or creamy, not both. However, powdered milk is an interesting ingredient that can help you bridge the divide, imparting richness and enabling volume, provided you use it correctly.

    Powdered milk can be made from skim milk, whole milk, and buttermilk, but all are essentially just milk with the water taken out and converted into a soluble powder. When it comes to water versus milk in scrambled eggs, folks typically favor the latter because it gives a bit of extra richness and flavor. However, it can weigh them down, unlike water, which steams to fluff up the little curds into pillowy softness. While you can't just add water to powdered milk eggs because you'd just be using milk with extra steps, it does allow you to employ other tricks that increase the fluffiness, giving you the best of both worlds.

    Powdered milk is also quite a bit more convenient since it's shelf-stable and dry. Not only does it last longer than regular milk, but you can also toast the powder to lend a nutty savoriness similar to browned butter. Roughly a tablespoon per three eggs is all you need to achieve serious flavor. Nonfat varieties typically last much longer than full-fat varieties, which tend to have a shorter shelf life. Freezing it can extend its shelf life even further, so it's an easy and cheap ingredient to keep on hand.

    The biggest benefit of powdered versus liquid milk is that it adds milk solids without adding extra water. This helps you avoid making your scrambled eggs too watery and is why, while it may not make them fluffy on its own, it also won't inhibit other tricks. There's no shortage of expert tips for restaurant-quality eggs, but try focusing on ones that add a bit of extra air and/or cook them quickly for the best results.

    You'll want to thoroughly incorporate your powdered milk, but luckily, a thorough whisking also helps introduce some air into the eggs. The goal is to make your mixture paler and more voluminous, looking as if you added extra liquid. The mason jar hack of shaking your eggs is not only easier than learning a fancy technique, but also helps ensure your powder is dispersed properly. If you're making a ton, you can even repurpose a protein shaker bottle and let that little metal whisk ball do the heavy lifting for you.

    Slowly bringing your eggs to temperature is a French style that gives them a creamy, porridge-like consistency. However, this also slowly coagulates the proteins and prevents them from fluffing up properly. The key is to cook them fast enough that their natural moisture steams, but not so hot that they turn rubbery. Full-fat milk powder can help contribute to a tender texture and, when used in conjunction with moderate heat, help produce eggs that are moist but fluffy, creamy but firm.

    #9595. Give Onion Rings A Protein Boost With This Breakfast Side

    Pairing your onion rings with a meaty ingredient doesn't just infuse them with umami, but can also make them a meal in their own right. Bacon-wrapped onion rings, in particular, are relatively straightforward to put together and have roughly 3 to 4 grams of protein per piece (depending on how much bacon each ring uses).

    Onions already have a dose of fiber, potassium, and vitamins C and B6, so adding some extra protein can give you something with a more comprehensive nutritional profile. While exact quantities vary based on the type, cut, and marbling of the bacon you use, meat is a "complete protein," meaning it contains all nine essential amino acids necessary for good health. Since this recipe doesn't call for deep-frying, it's not only easier, but also a good alternative for those attempting to reduce their consumption of vegetable-based oils. You won't even have to make sure any breading sticks, so it's a protein-laden option for those who want a bit of indulgence but steer clear of starches and grains.

    The recommended minimum dietary allowance for protein is 0.36 grams per pound of body weight, so getting your necessary amount every day can be a challenge. Finding little ways to introduce more into your diet, especially complete proteins, is a solid way to achieve this. Since leftover bacon reheats quite well, it's easy to make a batch of these onion rings ahead of time and have little protein snacks available throughout the week!

    Not all bacon is made equally, but you don't necessarily have to use the high-end slabs you can only find at a butcher shop. Just about anything will work, but some types are better for this recipe than others, and finding ways to use what you have is essential to tweaking it to your palate.

    When it comes to center versus thick-cut bacon, you may be better off using something on the thinner side. Even turkey bacon is a solid choice, with similar protein and less fat, but only if it's easy to work with. Cooking times vary quite a bit depending on your method — this could take 10 to 15 minutes in the air fryer, or up to an hour and a half on the grill if you're cooking over low heat — but you only have two real goals for this recipe. The first is giving the bacon a nice, crispy texture. The second is bringing the meat to a safe level of doneness, following the package instructions for pork or turkey bacon.

    If you're grilling, a toothpick or skewer is the best way to ensure your floppy bacon sticks to the onion ring, but your food can still be a bit delicate to move once it comes to room temperature. A quick trip to the fridge can help the meat stiffen enough to move onto the grill, where it should crisp and harden enough that it won't fall off quite so easily. This is also a good opportunity to let any additional seasoning soak into the meat, better infusing it with flavor.

    #9593. 19 non-traditional Thanksgiving desserts that aren't pie : Cakes, cookies, and even a tiramisu for your holiday dessert table.

    Yes, Thanksgiving is a pie-centric holiday. But what if you don’t like pie? Or maybe you just don’t want it. Either way, we’ve got lots of non-pie Thanksgiving desserts, from spiced pumpkin cupcakes to sugary apple cobblers, plus plenty of autumnal cakes.

    This adorable cake pulls double duty, serving as both a scene-stealing centerpiece and a feast-ending dessert. To make, stack two mini Bundt cakes together and frost with orange buttercream. Carving this frosted pumpkin at the end of the meal may just upstage the turkey!

    Get the recipe: The Great Pumpkin Bundt Cake

    To make this recipe, you’ll need: Mini Bundt Pan Set

    This dessert demonstrates how to dress up a crumb cake for fall: Top velvety sour cream cake with a juicy layer of apples, then crown the cake with a generous layer of apple pie-spiced streusel.

    To make this recipe, you'll need: Instant Clearjel

    Cranberry sauce can be a polarizing side dish, but everyone will love this New England-inspired cake, which pairs tart cranberries with walnuts and vanilla for a simple, satisfying dessert. (Because it’s so quick to make, this is a particularly good recipe for any last-minute holiday baking.)

    To make this recipe, you’ll need: Sparkling Sugar

    Sweet potatoes belong on the dessert table, and this recipe proves it. This ultra-soft cake is gently spiced and glows orange from the sweet potato purée, and it’s finished with a fluffy meringue that mimics marshmallow-topped sweet potato casseroles.

    Get the recipe: Sweet Potato Sheet Cake with Marshmallow Frosting (make it gluten-free with Measure for Measure Flour)

    To make this recipe, you’ll need: 9” x 13” pan

    For a dessert that’s rich but not too sweet, turn to this recipe, which pairs pumpkin and pumpkin spice with chocolate chips. Baked in a decorative Bundt pan, it can be served unfrosted for an easy-yet-elegant dessert.

    Get the recipe: Pumpkin-Chocolate Chip Cake

    To make this recipe, you’ll need: Soft Swirl Bundt Pan

    Instead of apple pie, try an apple pan dowdy on your Thanksgiving dessert table. The pan dowdy is a traditional American dish from the 1800s and early 1900s. A combination of pie and pudding, the name comes from the method in which the recipe is completed: After an apple-based filling is baked in a crust-lined casserole, the baker takes a fork and "dowdies" the crust, breaking it into pieces that remain crisp despite being partially immersed in the juicy filling.

    To make this recipe, you’ll need: 9" square pan

    “Thanksgiving cheesecake” may not have quite the same ring as “Thanksgiving pie,” but when your guests are eating this ultra-creamy dessert, they won’t care. With its burnished top and custardy interior, this Pumpkin Basque Cheesecake reimagines the classic with bold autumnal flair, thanks to golden pumpkin purée and warm spices.

    Get the recipe: Pumpkin Basque Cheesecake

    To make this recipe, you’ll need: Pumpkin Pie Spice

    Don’t be fooled by its stodgy name or humble appearance: This cake is so good, we named it our #1 best fall recipe! In fact, my colleague Jessica Battilana made it for Thanksgiving last year and declared it the biggest hit of the day; her guests fell in love with the moist, apple-loaded cake and fudgy brown sugar frosting.

    Get the recipe: Old-Fashioned Apple Cake with Brown Sugar Frosting

    To make this recipe, you’ll need: Vermont Boiled Cider

    If your biggest complaint about PSLs is that there's not enough coffee flavor, look to this Bundt cake, which has an espresso powder swirl running through the tender pumpkin crumb and a coffee glaze to finish the whole thing off.

    Get the recipe: Pumpkin Espresso Bundt Cake

    To make this recipe, you'll need: Golden Wheat Flour

    If you don’t want to fuss with pie, we suggest making a cobbler instead. This fruit-filled version pairs juicy spiced apples with a crackly brown sugar crust — both prep and serving are easy, and the resulting cobbler will absolutely steal the show.

    Get the recipe: Sugar-Crusted Apple Cobbler

    To make this recipe, you’ll need: Vietnamese Cinnamon

    Apples are great, but seasonal pears deserve some love too. This simple cake, made with a combination of almond and all-purpose flours, has a rich, buttery texture and an almost marzipan-like chew. Studded with fragrant cubes of ripe pear, it's an elegant after-dinner dessert.

Pecans are blended into the crust to add a subtle nutty flavor and delicate crunch. If you really want to level up your presentation, check out these cupcake decorating techniques for a pro-level finish.

    #9591. Cranberry Brie Wontons

    If your friends love our cranberry brie bites, they’ll go nuts for these cranberry brie wontons. Brushed with butter and air-fried until crispy on the outside and gooey in the middle, these wontons are the party snack you need this holiday season. Don’t forget the bowl of cranberry sauce for dunking—it makes it feel extra-festive.

    Stuffing the wontons:In order to have a satisfactorily cheesy center after the wontons are fried, you’ll need to cram a lot of brie into the wonton when stuffing it. Brie shrinks a lot when it melts, so while a 1/2-ounce cube might feel like a lot, it’s actually the perfect amount.

    Cooking the wontons:While wontons are often deep-fried, I opted for the air fryer here since it makes for faster, easier cleanup and still yields a delicious result. Yes, the wontons don’t get quite as bubble-textured or evenly browned as they would if they were deep-fried, but they still crisp up really nicely—and the butter adds a delightful flavor all on its own!

    Make-ahead tips:Once cooked, these wontons are best eaten immediately. But if you want to make ahead, you can form and freeze the wontons for up to 1 month. Freeze on a parchment-lined baking sheet until hard, then transfer to an airtight container. Wontons that have been totally frozen might take a few extra minutes to air-fry!

    #9590. This Thanksgiving, make your pies mini: Mini pies may be the secret to a stress-free celebration.

    What’s the one food you most look forward to at Thanksgiving?

    For some it’s the turkey. For others it’s the array of sides. But for many of us bakers, let’s admit it — our thoughts skip right over the apps and main meal and go straight to the pies, whether it's apple, pumpkin, pecan, or all of them together.

    The problem is that for smaller gatherings, the need for multiple pies diminishes. Still, how can you bear to choose between apple, pumpkin, and pecan?

    Enter the mini pie, a great way to showcase an array of pies and have them all disappear by the end of the day.

    Here’s a potential hosting scenario this year: You’re serving six close family members (including yourself) at Thanksgiving dinner; you want to offer pumpkin, apple, and pecan pie. So you pull out your mini muffin pan and use it to make mini pies in a variety of different flavors. Everyone can enjoy one mini pie immediately, one later, and squirrel one away for the next day.

    And mini pies aren't just handy for smaller gatherings — they can also make life a little easier during the frenetic rush of food prep in the days before Turkey Day. Helpfully, you can make these pies well ahead of Thanksgiving; they can be prepared, baked, and then frozen for up to a few weeks before serving.

    Once cool, wrap each pie individually in plastic, then bag them all airtight and freeze. When you’re ready to serve, unwrap, thaw, and reheat briefly: 5 to 10 minutes in a 350°F oven or about 20 seconds (per pie) in a microwave will bring them back to life.

    Because these mini pies have a higher crust-to-filling ratio, you don't need to prebake the crust to avoid a soggy bottom. Just place the pie dough rounds in your mini muffin pan, fill with about a tablespoon of the pumpkin custard, and bake.

    Another benefit: The smaller amount of filling makes it easier to nail the bake. You don't have to look for a perfect amount of jiggle in your pie before removing from the oven — just bake until the exposed edges are golden brown and the custard is set in the center.

    Turn to our Pecan Tassies recipe — a beloved Southern dessert, pecan tassies are basically just bite-size pecan pies. This recipe uses a tender, unsweetened cream cheese pastry, which cradles a gooey nut filling sweetened with brown sugar (no corn syrup).

    We’ve saved perhaps the most beloved pie for last: apple. These mini apple pies are a bit more involved than the pumpkin or pecan pies. You need to precook the filling, and you have to choose how to top them. That said, they’re totally worth the effort (and the filling can be prepared up to five days in advance; store the cooled filling, covered, in the refrigerator until ready to bake).

    Once you've precooked the diced apple filling on the stovetop to remove excess liquid, assemble your pies in your mini muffin pan by lining with rounds of pie dough and adding the apples. You can then choose how to top them:

    You may be questioning whether making mini Thanksgiving pies is more trouble than it's worth. But helpfully, the techniques involved are very approachable — mix, roll, fill, bake — and the resulting pies are both delicious and just plain fun. Have you ever wanted a whole Thanksgiving pie just for yourself? You can have it — in miniature. Happy baking!

    Do you say you won't dare bake pie because you're unsure of your skills with a rolling pin? Check out these other easy no-roll crusts: No-Roll Pie Crust and Graham Cracker Crust.

    #9587. Aggressive Policing as a Public Health Issue

    The medical field has paid increased attention to the negative health impacts of systemic racism, discrimination, poverty, and other societal forces that are known to cause poorer health. This includes awareness of the need to assess and address racial and other health disparities and focus on principles of diversity, equity, and inclusion. We have moved beyond the framing of these issues as moral imperatives to understanding how they are related to individual and public health.

    Discussion of the health harms of aggressive policing has also increased over the last 2 years, spurred by the frequent and well-publicized deaths of Black, Indigenous, and people of color (BIPOC). What has been viewed as a political issue is now understood as a public health/health inequity concern. Two articles that have helped change the way the medical community views these issues were published in 2021:

    Both of these pieces help illustrate the ongoing shift in how police violence and aggressive policing have specific and disproportionate impacts on communities of color.

    The first article makes several key points in its assertion that policing concerns should be viewed as health issues. It begins with this statement:

    “Marginalized communities have a long history of naming the systemic racism and harms of police violence to health and well-being and recognizing their roots in the oppression of Black and Indigenous communities.”

    The article cites data indicating that BIPOC are far more likely to be killed by police than White Americans, noting that death at the hands of a police officer is the sixth leading cause of death for young Black men. Similarly, Black and Indigenous women are more likely to be killed by a police officer than their White counterparts.

    The second article also looks at specific data related to the disparate impact of what is describes as the “overexposure” to aggressive policing strategies among Black communities, serving to increase already existing health disparities in such communities. The article authors noted:

    “Indeed, aggressive policing strategies employed by law enforcement agencies across the country have been hypothesized to degrade health and well-being, even among people who themselves have not experienced contact with police. Perhaps even more important, aggressive policing is thought to contribute to significant population health inequities, as these practices are concentrated on — and thus exacerbate — the health challenges faced by racialized populations.”

    The authors of the article cited data from an organization called Campaign Zero.3 This group’s website includes data that also helps demonstrated the negative impact of aggressive policing, or what they describe as “broken windows” policing. This form of policing has led to the overpolicing of communities of color with resulting excessive force, leading to unnecessary deaths.

    “Meanwhile, the vast majority of arrests are for low-level, nonviolent activities in encounters that often escalate to deadly force. For example, in 2014, police killed at least 287 people who were involved in minor offenses and harmless activities like sleeping in parks, possessing drugs, looking “suspicious” or having a mental health crisis. These activities are often symptoms of underlying issues of drug addiction, homelessness, and mental illness, which should be treated by health care professionals and social workers rather than the police.”

    These 3 examples of the evolving understanding of how to view police aggressiveness highlight the need for future research and data collection. They also highlight the need for PAs, nurse practitioners, and other medical providers to assess the health impact of high-impact policing on their patients and to advocate for changes to a policing system that results in furthering existing health disparities.

    1. Fleming PJ, Lopez WD, Spolum M, Anderson RE, Reyes AG, Schulz AJ. Policing is a public health issue: the important role of health educators. Health Educ Behav. 2021:10901981211001010. doi:10.1177/10901981211001010

    2. Esposito M, Larimore S, Lee H. Aggressive policing, health, and health equity. Health Policy Brief. Health Affairs. April 30, 2021. doi:10.1377/hpb20210412.997570.

    3. Campaign Zero. https://www.joincampaignzero.org/solutions#solutionsoverview

    This article originally appeared on Clinical Advisor

    Psychiatry Advisor, a trusted source of medical news and feature content for healthcare providers, offers clinicians insight into the latest research to inform clinical practice and improve patient outcomes.
